One of the greatest issues of this IMO problem is that one may not construct a diagram without having solved some part of it. Most of the solutions above overcome this by taking the reflections of $C$ with respect to $B$ and $D$ , or some equivalent stuff. This solution, which I found along with a friend of mine, explores another approach to this "unconstructability". Let $Q$ and $R$ be the orthogonal projections of $C$ onto $HS$ and $HT$ , respectively. $\angle{CQS}=\angle{SBC}=90^{\circ}$ yields that $QSBC$ is cyclic; moreover, $\angle{QHC}=180^{\circ}-\angle{CHS}=180^{\circ}-(90^{\circ}+\angle{CSB})=90^{\circ}-\angle{CSB}=\angle{BCS}=\angle{BQS}$ . Therefore, if $M=BQ\cap CH$ then $MQ=MH$ ; since $\angle{CQH}$ is right, $M$ is the midpoint of $CH$ . And now we may actually draw the diagram: simply construct the midpoint $M$ of $CH$ , choose $Q$ on $BM$ such that $MQ=MH$ and set $S=HQ\cap AB$ . The construction of point $T$ is analogous. Now we claim that $MB=MD$ . By Stewart, this is equivalent to $2BH^2+2BC^2-CH^2=2DH^2+2DC^2-CH^2$ , or, equivalently, to $BH^2-DH^2=DC^2-BC^2$ . But $AC^2=BC^2+AB^2=DC^2+AD^2$ , thus $DC^2-BC^2=AB^2-AD^2=(AB^2-AH^2)-(AD^2-AH^2)=BH^2-DH^2$ , and we're done with our claim. Since $MQ=MR$ , lines $QR$ and $BD$ are parallel. Now everything is reduced to a standard geometry problem on triangle $HRQ$ . Point $M$ is the circumcenter, point $C$ is diametrally opposite to $H$ , $B$ and $D$ are simply the intersection points of $QM$ and $RM$ with the paralel to $QR$ through $H$ ; $S$ is the intersection point of the perpendicular to $BC$ through $B$ with $HQ$ ; $T$ is constructed in an analogous way. By Pythagoras, $CS^2=BS^2+BC^2=QS^2+QC^2$ . Cosine law yields $BS^2=HS^2+HB^2-2\cdot HS\cdot HB\cos(\angle{DHQ})=HS^2+HB^2-2\cdot HS\cdot HB\cos(\angle{RQH})$ . Moreover, $QS=QH+HS$ . Now use this in the above equality to get $HS^2+HB^2-2\cdot HS\cdot HB\cos(\angle{RQH})+HB^2=HS^2+QH^2+2\cdot QH\cdot HB+QC^2$ . stem_md: Let  $n \ge 2$  be an integer. Consider an  $n \times n$  chessboard consisting of  $n^2$  unit squares. A configuration of  $n$  rooks on this board is *peaceful* if every row and every column contains exactly one rook. Find the greatest positive integer  $k$  such that, for each peaceful configuration of  $n$  rooks, there is a  $k \times k$  square which does not contain a rook on any of its  $k^2$  unit squares.
solution_md:
The answer is  $k=\lceil \sqrt{n}\rceil-1$  (and what a surprising one too!).**Proving that  $k=\lceil \sqrt{n}\rceil-1$  works.**

If  $k=\lceil \sqrt{n}\rceil-1$ , then  $k<\sqrt{n}$ . Let  $n=ak+b$  where  $0\leq b<k$ . Now consider an  $ak\times ak$  sub-board of the  $n\times n$  board and divide this sub-board into non-overlapping square grids of side length  $k$ . We see that we can make  $a^2\geq\frac{n^2}{k^2}=\frac{n}{k^2}\cdot n>n$  square grids, so not all of them can be filled with rooks. Thus one of these  $k\times k$  squares does not contain any rook.  $\square$ **Showing that  $k>\lceil \sqrt{n}\rceil-1$  fails.**

It suffices to show that  $k=\lceil \sqrt{n}\rceil$  does not work for some configuration of rooks, since for that configuration, any  $k>\lceil \sqrt{n}\rceil$  also does not work. Let $k=\lceil \sqrt{n}\rceil$ . Then let  $n=k\cdot l+m$  where  $0\leq m<k$ . Note that  $n\geq k\cdot l\geq \sqrt{n}\cdot l$ , so  $l\leq \sqrt{n}\leq k$ . Now consider the  $lk\times lk$  sub-board of the  $n\times n$  board, that contains the top left square of the original board. Divide this sub-board into  $l^2$  squares of side length  $k$ . Also label the columns of this sub-board with numbers  $1,2,3,...$  successively where column  $1$  is the left-most column. Now consider the following algorithm: $\bullet$  At step  $i$ , consider the columns numbered  $(i-1)k+1,(i-1)k+2,\dots, ik$ , and place  $l$  rooks such that each rook is on a different column as well as a different  $k\times k$  square. This can be done since  $l\leq k$ . We do this for  $i=1,2,\dots, l$ .  $\bullet$  For step  $i>1$ , also ensure that the rooks do not share a row with any of the rooks placed in step  $i-1$ . This can be done, since till step  $i-1$ , only  $i-1$  rows which pass through a particular  $k\times k$  square is occupied, and so, in step  $i$  we can always choose an unoccupied row passing through each  $k\times k$  square till the end of the algorithm (since  $i\leq l\leq k$ ).

After this algorithm is over, we can place the remaining rooks (if there are any) on the remaining squares of the  $n\times n$  board peacefully. Now note that inside the  $lk\times lk$  sub-board, there are no rook-free  $k\times k$  squares. Outside this sub-board, the largest square grid has dimension  $m\times m$  and  $m<k$  as assumed before, and so there are no  $k\times k$  rook-free squares in this peaceful configuration.  $\square$ Thus our answer is  $\boxed{\lceil \sqrt{n}\rceil-1}$ .  $\blacksquare$

My approach for this problem.
Step 1. FInd the lower bound of  $k$  in term of  $n$ .
COnsider the  $\left\lfloor\tfrac{n}{k+1}\right\rfloor ^2(k+1)^2$ -sized sub-square in the top left corner of the initial board. Divide this subsquare to smaller  $(k+1)^2$ -squares; each has at least one rook, so the sub-square has at least  $\left\lfloor\tfrac{n}{k+1}\right\rfloor ^2$  rooks. On the other hand, the sub-square has  $\left\lfloor\tfrac{n}{k+1}\right\rfloor (k+1)$  columns, so it has at most that number of rooks. Hence:  $$ \left\lfloor\frac{n}{k+1}\right\rfloor\leq k+1. $$  In the strictly inequality case, we have  $\tfrac{n}{k+1}<k+1\implies n<(k+1)^2$ . In the equality case, we have  $n=(k+1)^2+r \text{ with } 0\leq r\leq k$ . We shall prove that  $r>0$  is impossible. Indeed, we extend the edges of the  $(k+1)^2\times (k+1)^2$  sub-square so that they cut the edge of the initial board, create an addition  $r\times r$  sub-square. Since we have equality, the  $(k+1)^2\times (k+1)^2$  sub-square has exactly  $(k+1)^2$  rooks so the  $r\times  r$  square contains the remaining  $r$  rooks. Now, switch the  $(k+1)^2\times (k+1)^2$  sub-square to the adjacent corner and keep the rooks in their places. Extend its edges and a new  $r\times r$  is created. Analogously, this  $r\times r$  square also has  $r$  rooks, this is a contradiction, since the two  $r\times r$  squares share their rows.  $\square$ We proved that  $n\leq (k+1)^2$ .
Step 2: Find the upper bound of  $k$ .
If  $n=m^2$ , then divide the board into  $m\times m$  squares.  Put the rooks in the board in the  $(mi+j, mj+i)$  positions. One can easily find that the peaceful config is established, and each  $m\times m$  square has exactly one rook, so  $k^2\leq (m-1)^2<n$ .
If  $m^2<n<(m+1)^2$ , we extend the board to the  $(m+1)^2\times (m+1)^2$  board. Put the rooks in the new board in the way described above. Now take any sub-board of size  $n\times n$ . The remaining rooks can always be arranged in the empty rows so that the peaceful config is setted. So  $k^2\leq m^2<n$ .  $\square$ We have proved that:  $$ k^2<n\leq (k+1)^2\iff k=\lfloor\sqrt{n-1}\rfloor. $$

Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. Consider an $n \times n$ chessboard consisting of $n^2$ unit squares. A configuration of $n$ rooks on this board is *peaceful* if every row and every column contains exactly one rook. Find the greatest positive integer $k$ such that, for each peaceful configuration of $n$ rooks, there is a $k \times k$ square which does not contain a rook on any of its $k^2$ unit squares.

Basically, there are $k+1$ rows between two consecutive rooks. To see that we can find a $k \times k$ square, consider a $n \times k$ rectangle whose bottom row has a rook on it. Then we have a $(n-1) \times k$ rectangle above the bottom $1 \times k$ rectangle. Note that the number of disjoint $k \times k$ squares in this top rectangle is $\frac{n-1}{k} \ge k.$ On the other hand, there are $k$ columns and one column is already occupied (by the rook in the bottom row), and so this rectangle will only have $k-1$ rooks on it. The answer is $\boxed{\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor}$ for nonsquare $n,$ and $\boxed{\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor - 1}$ for square $n.$ Let $n$ be a nonsquare positive integer. Then, if $k = \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor - 1,$ it is possible to partition the $n \times n$ board into $(\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor + 1)^2$ disjoint subsquares each of length and width $\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor - 1.$ This is because $( \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor + 1 )( \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor - 1 ) = \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor ^2 - 1 \leq n.$ Now suppose there is a peaceful configuration that does not contain a $k \times k$ empty squares. However, this means each of those $(\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor + 1)^2$ must contain a rook, but this would be more than $n$ rooks. Thus, this value of $k$ is good. Now we show that $k = \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor = m$ is also good. Let $n = m^2 + j,$ where $m^2$ is the largest square less than $n$ and $j > 0.$ Consider the topmost $m$ rows of the board. By the pigeonhole principle, it takes at least $m+1$ rooks to be placed in these rows, so that number of columns between pairs of closest rooks and rooks to the left/right edge of the board is always at most $m-1.$ (Otherwise, there'd be an $m \times m$ open empty square in the top $m$ rows of the board.) However, if this is true, again by pigeonhole, there'd be two rooks in the same column, as $m+1 > m.$ This is not peaceful, so it is not possible in this case to cover $m$ squares. Therefore, we've show that $k = m = \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor$ is good. To show that $k \leq \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor,$ we observe the configuration as follows, which clearly generalizes to any $n.$ Label the chessboard as $(r, c)$ representing row, column, respectively. Then starting with a rook at $(1,1)$ move down one row and change the column to the previous column value plus $\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor$ , modded by $n.$ Do this all the way down the $n$ rows of the board. Note that in this configuration, between any two closest rooks, there is at most $\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor$ rows/columns between them, and similarly between the edge of the grid and rooks. Thus, there is no side length $\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor + 1$ square of emptiness in this configuration, so we've shown $k \leq \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor,$ so the maximum value for nonsquare $n$ is $k = \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor.$

The answer is \(k=\left\lfloor\sqrt{n-1}\right\rfloor\). The proof contains two steps:

\bigskip**Proof \(k=\left\lfloor\sqrt{n-1}\right\rfloor\) works:** Let \(n=k^2+a\). Assume without loss of generality the rook in the bottom row is not in the bottom \(a\times a\) square (otherwise reflect), so the bottom \(a\times a\) square contains at most \(a-1\) rooks. If the bottom \(a\times a\) square contains \(a-i\) rooks, \(i\ge1\), then the bottom-left \(a\cdot k^2\) rectangle contains \(i\) rooks, and so does the top-right \(k^2\cdot a\) rectangle.

Hence the top-left \(k^2\times k^2\) square contains \(k^2-i<k^2\) rooks. Split the \(k^2\times k^2\) grid into \(k^2\) smaller \(k\times k\) grids; by Pigeonhole, one of these \(k\times k\) grid contains no rook.

\bigskip**Proof \(k^2\ge n\) fail:** We will construct a \(n\times n\) grid where every \(k\times k\) square contains a rook.

We will take cases on whether we there exists a size  $k \times k$  square that is empty:

Case 1:  $k \leq \lfloor\sqrt{n-1}\rfloor$  works. 
Proof: Consider the top  $k$  rows of the square, and tile them with  $k$   $k\times k$  squares such that there is no room between consecutive squares (there can be room between the final square and the right side of the grid). Now note that we need a rook in each of these squares. Also, since we have  $k^2+1 \leq n$ , we can shift the rightmost  $k \times k$  square over by one row. Now we need a rook in each square of this configuration, but since we also needed a rook in each square in the previous configuration, there must exist a rook in the common tiles of the two squares (the rightmost one before and after shifting). Also note that these tiles span exactly  $k-1$  rows. 

Now the key thing is to note that we can repeat this  $k$  times since  $k^2 \leq n$ , so we can just shift this configuration down  $k$  rows and repeat. But since, in each configuration, we must have a rook in one of those  $k-1$  rows, we must have  $k$  rooks in  $k-1$  rows - a contradiction. 

Case 2:  $k > \lfloor\sqrt{n-1}\rfloor$  doesn't work. 
Proof: First, it suffices to show that  $m=\lfloor\sqrt{n-1}\rfloor+1$  doesn't work, so we will do so. We can consider the construction mentioned from @above, i.e. put a rook in the top-leftmost tile, then move right one column and down  $m$  rows, and repeat. And if we go outside the grid, we will move to the next column and start at the highest row that is empty. It is easy to see that this works, but to be concrete:

We assume that there exists some  $m \times m$  square that is empty, and we show this is impossible through contradiction. 
Now note that rooks in the  $m$  rows the square takes up must be either above or below the square. But by the nature of the construction, there exist two rooks such that the number of rows (one can start under the  $m \times m$  square and "wrap up" to the top) between them is least  $m(m-1)+1=m^2-m+1$  so in total, we have that \[(m^2-m+1)+m =m^2+1 \leq n\]a contradiction, so we are done.</details>

First we show that any  $n\times n$  peaceful configuration has an empty  $ k \times k $  square for  $k = \lfloor \sqrt{n - 1} \rfloor$ . We show that if  $n = a^2 + b$  for some  $0< b \le 2a + 1$ , then there is an empty  $a\times a $  square in an  $n\times n $  peaceful configuration. Suppose there was not such an  $a\times a $  empty square. 

Claim: Every corner square has a rook on it. 
Proof: Suppose not for some corner square. WLOG the corner square is the lower right. Then there are in total two rooks contained in the union of the rightmost column and bottommost row. This implies that there are  $a^2 - 1$  squares contained in the top  $a^2 \times a^2$  sub board. However, we can partition this sub board into  $a^2$  disjoint  $a\times a$  squares, so one of them must not have a rook in them, absurd.  $\square$ Now, this implies there are two squares in the same row that both have a rook on them, which is absurd. Therefore, there must be such an  $a\times a$  empty square, as desired. 

We now prove that for  $n = a^2+ b$  with  $0<b\le 2a + 1$  that there exists a  $n\times n$  peaceful configuration with no empty  $(a+1) \times (a + 1)$  square. 

Claim: If there exists a peaceful configuration with no empty  $(a+1) \times (a+1)$  square for  $k$ , then there also exists one for  $k - 1$ . 
Proof: Consider removing a row and column that both have a corner cell in it (they are on the edge of the board). There is a  $(k-1) \times (k-1)$  board remaining without any empty  $(a+1)\times (a+1)$  square. If this board has  $k - 1$  cells, then it must be peaceful, so we are done. If it has  $k - 2$  cells, then there must be both a row and column that was never hit, so adding a cell in the intersection of that row and column gives a peaceful configuration for  $k - 1$ , which still obviously has no empty  $(a+1) \times (a+1)$  squares.  $\square$ Therefore, it suffices to show that an  $(a+1)^2 \times (a+1)^2$  has a peaceful configuration without any empty  $(a+1) \times (a+1)$  squares, or in other words, an  $(x^2) \times (x^2)$  board has a peaceful configuration without any  $x\times x $  square. Give each square coordinates, where the bottom left cell has coordinate  $(1,1)$  and the top right has coordinate  $(x^2, x^2)$ . Let  $S = \{(1,1), (x+1, 2), (2x+1,3) \ldots, (x^2 - x + 1, x)\}$ . Define adding coordinates  $(a,b)$  and  $(c,d)$  to be  $(a+c, b + d)$ . 

Consider the construction  $S \cup (S + (1,x)) \cup (S + (2,2x)) \cup (S + (x-1, x^2 - x) )$ . It can be checked that no two  $x$ -coordinates intersect and no two  $y$ -coordinates intersect, so this configuration is peaceful. We can also see that there are no empty  $x\times x$  squares in this configuration also, as desired.

We claim that the answer is  $\boxed{k=\lfloor\sqrt{n-1}\rfloor}$ . 
We first show that there must always exists a  $k\times k$  'free' square in the arrangement. A free  $k\times k$  square is a square of size  $k\times k$  such that none of its cells has any rook. 
Consider  $k$  adjacent columns. Let the  $k$  rooks be numbered according to their row number (starting from  $1$ ). Suppose the numbers are  $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_k$  such that  $1\leq a_1<a_2<\ldots<a_k\leq n+1=a_{k+1}$ . Since the numbers are listed in an increasing order, then for any  $1\leq i<j\leq n+1$ , we have  $a_j-a_i>k$  if and only if there exists a  $k\times k$  empty square. Supppose there was no  $k\times k$  empty square. Then, the following inequalities hold: $a_2-a_1\leq k$ ,  $\ldots$ ,  $n+1-a_k\leq k$ Adding the  $k$  inequalities, we get  $n+1-a_1\leq k^2\leq n-1\Longrightarrow a_1\geq2$ , which contradicts the existence of a rook in the first row. The bound is therefore correct.

We now provide a construction where every  $(k+1)\times(k+1)$  square is covered. Suppose that for each  $1\leq i\leq n$ , we place the rook at column  $i$  and row  $\pi_i$ . Here,  $\pi=(\pi_1,\pi_2,\ldots,\pi_n)$  is a permutation of  $(1,2,\ldots,n)$ . Let  $k=\lfloor\sqrt{n-1}\rfloor$ . Then, if  $\gcd(n,k+1)=1$ , the permutation is set as  $a_1=1$  and  $a_{i+1}\equiv a_i+k+1\pmod{n}$ , for each  $1\leq i<n$ . Moreover, if  $\gcd(n,k+1)\ne1$  then  $\gcd(n+1,k+1)=1$ , and since  $a_1=1$ , we simply delete the first row and first column. However, this does not work when  $n$  is a perfect square as  $n=(k+1)^2$ . In that case, we follow the contruction for  $n-1$ , and add a new column at bottommost and new row at rightmost end, and a   rook is placed at row  $n$  and column  $n$ . 
Note that the value of  $k$  obtained for these constructions are weakly increasing. So, if we just prove the constructions for the perfect squares, we are done. 
The arrangement of rooks obtained for  $n=(k+1)^2$  is \[(1,1), (2,k+2), (3,2k+3),\ldots, (k+1,k^2+k+1),(k+2,2),(k+3,k+4),\ldots,(2k+2,k^2+k+2),(2k+3,3),\ldots,(n,n)\]
Here rook in row  $j$  and column  $i$  is placed at  $(i,j)$ . 
This works because for any rook, the distance (parallel or perpendicular to the sides of the square) between its adjacent rooks is  $k$ . This is because the rooks nearest to  $(ik+i+j,jk+i+1-k)$  are  $((i-1)k+(i-1)+j,jk+i+1-k),((i+1)k+i+1+j,jk+i+2-k),(ik+i+j-1,(j-1)k+i+1-k),(ik+i+j+1,jk+i+1)$ So, there is no  $(k+1)\times(k+1)$  free triangle.
The proof is complete.  $\blacksquare$

I claim that no good subset can contain 0, or  $k^2$  for that matter from symmetry, which would finish. If it did contain  $0$ , then the "highest" we can climb using our rows is  $k(k-1)$ . However, at the end we have  $k^2 - k(k-1) = k$  empty rows which leaves an empty  $k \times k$  square. Contradiction. 

Notice that it is possible to place rooks on a  $k^2+1$  grid that covers all  $k+1$  grids. Additionally, we can place rooks on a  $k^2$  grid that covers all  $k$  grids. I will omit constructions here. Notice that rooks on a  $k^2$  grid cannot cover all the  $k-1$  grids because there are not enough rooks. This coupled with the nondecreasing condition finishes.

Our answer is  $\boxed{\lceil \sqrt n - 1 \rceil}$ . For  $n$  perfect square, use the construction where the board is divided into a matrix of  $\sqrt n \times \sqrt n$  squares, and for the square in position  $(i,j)$  of this matrix, place a rook in position  $(j,i)$  of that square. For  $n$  not perfect square, use a subgrid of the next highest perfect square board.

Let  $a = \lceil \sqrt n - 1 \rceil$ . To show that there must exist an empty  $a \times a$  square, we consider an  $n \times a$  subgrid which contains the leftmost rook on the chessboard. We have an  $(n-1) \times a$  subgrid containing  $a-1$  rooks, from which we see that the "horizontal distance" (number of empty columns in this subgrid) between some two consecutive rooks is guaranteed to be at least
\[\left\lceil \frac{n-1 - (a-1)}{(a-1) + 1} \right\rceil = a,\]

giving us our empty  $a \times a$  square.  $\blacksquare$

We claim the optimum is achieved at  $k = \lfloor \sqrt{n - 1} \rfloor$ . It suffices to show that for  $k = \lfloor \sqrt{n - 1} \rfloor + 1$ , there exists a rook configuration that contradicts the problem statement, and that for  $k = \lfloor \sqrt{n - 1} \rfloor$  we can always find a  $k \times k$  subgrid of the chessboard with no rooks.

First, we will show that there exists a configuration for  $k = \lfloor \sqrt{n - 1} \rfloor + 1$  where every  $k \times k$  subgrid contains a rook. For brevity, assign vector lattice coordinates  $\langle i, j \rangle$  for  $0 \le i, j \le n - 1$  to the centers of square of the  $n \times n$  chessboard. Consider vectors  $\textbf{u} = \langle k, 1 \rangle, \textbf{v} = \langle1, k \rangle$ . We can place rooks on all squares centered on vectors of the form  $a \textbf{u} + b \textbf{v}$  over all integers  $0 \le a, b \le \left \lceil \dfrac{n}{k} \right\rceil - 1$ , which works by inspection.

Now let  $k = \lfloor \sqrt{n - 1} \rfloor$ . We will prove that an empty  $k \times k$  subgrid always exists in the chessboard. Define row  $i$  as the row with  $i - 1$  rows below it, and define column  $i$  as the row with  $i - 1$  columns to the left of it. Since the configuration is peaceful, and the conditions of the problem are preserved by a reflection over the vertical midline, WLOG there exists an  $x \le \dfrac{n + 1}{2}$  such that column  $x$  contains a rook in row  $1$ .

Consider the whole collection of columns  $x, x + 1, \cdots, x + k - 1$ , and let  $a_i$  be the row that the rook in column  $x + i - 1$  is in. We can relabel the whole set  $\{a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_n \}$  in increasing order  $b_1 < b_2 < \cdots < b_n$ . It suffices to show that there exists some  $i$  where  $b_{i + 1} - b_i \ge k + 1$  or  $n - b_n \ge k$ . For the sake of contradiction, assume this is false. Then
\[b_2 - b_1 \le k ~~ , ~~  b_3 - b_2 \le k ~~ , ~~ \cdots ~~, ~~  b_k - b_{k - 1} \le k ~~ , ~~  n - b_k \le k - 1 \]
but since  $b_1 = 1$ , we can sum all of these relations up and obtain  $n \le k^2$  which is clearly false for  $k = \lfloor \sqrt{n - 1} \rfloor$ . Thus we reach a contradiction, and we are done.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md:
Let  $a_0 < a_1 < a_2 < \dots$  be an infinite sequence of positive integers. Prove that there exists a unique integer  $n\geq 1$  such that
\[a_n < \frac{a_0+a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_n}{n} \leq a_{n+1}.\]

*Proposed by Gerhard Wöginger, Austria.*
solution_md:
<details><summary>solution</summary>Call the entire inequality  $(*).$  Suppose there is no such  $n$  satisfying  $(*).$  This means that if the left inequality for a particular  $n$  holds, then the right inequality must fail. Clearly, the left inequality is true for  $n=1.$ Then, this implies  $a_1 < \frac{a_0 + a_1}{1} \Longrightarrow a_0 + a_1 \nleq a_2 \Longrightarrow a_2 < a_0 + a_1 \Longrightarrow 2a_2 < a_0 + a_1 + a_2 \Longrightarrow a_2 < \frac{a_0 + a_1 + a_2}{2},$   $\Longrightarrow a_3 < \frac{a_0 + a_1 + a_2}{2} \Longrightarrow a_3 < \frac{a_0 + a_1 + a_2}{2} \Longrightarrow 3a_3 < a_0 + a_1 + a_2 + a_3 \Longrightarrow a_3 < \frac{a_0 + a_1 + a_2 + a_3}{3}$   $\Longrightarrow a_4 < \frac{a_0 + a_1 + a_2 + a_3}{3} \Longrightarrow 4a_4 < a_0 + a_1 + a_2 + a_3 + a_4 \Longrightarrow a_4 < \frac{a_0 + a_1 + a_2 + a_3 + a_4}{4},$  and so forth.

Using the inequality  $a_{n+1} < \frac{a_0 + a_1 + \cdots + a_n}{n} \Longleftrightarrow a_{n+1} <  \frac{a_0 + a_1  +\cdots + a_n + a_{n+1}}{n+1},$  we now see that by induction, if  $(*)$  is false, then the left inequality is always true and right inequality is always false, as these each imply each other (Left inequality for  $n=k$  is true  $\Longrightarrow$  Right inequality for  $n=k$  is false  $\Longrightarrow$  Left inequality for  $n=k+1$  is true, so forth). This implies then that we must have  $\boxed{a_n < a_{n+1} < \frac{a_0 + a_1 + \cdots + a_n}{n} \hspace{0.3cm} (**)} ,$  for all  $n \geq 1.$ However, note that for sufficiently large  $n \geq a_0,$  and observing that  $a_{n+1} \geq a_n + 1,$  we have  $n(a_n + 1) = n a_n + n \geq (a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n) + a_0 \Longleftrightarrow \frac{a_0 + a_1 + \cdots + a_n}{n} \leq a_n + 1 \leq a_{n+1},$  contradicting  $(**).$ Thus, we have contradicted the original assumption that there are no solutions to  $(*),$  and there exists such  $n.$  We now show that this  $n$  is unique. Suppose that for some  $k,$  we have \[a_k < \frac{a_0+a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_k}{k} \leq a_{k+1}. \]Then, we deduce: $a_{k+1} \geq \frac{a_0 + a_1 + ... + a_k}{k} \Longrightarrow a_{k+1} \geq \frac{a_0 + a_1 + ... + a_{k+1}}{k+1},$  and in general, we have inductively  $a_{n} \geq \frac{a_0 + a_1 + ... + a_n}{n},$  for all  $n \geq k+1.$  Then, the left inequality always fails for larger  $n,$  and, we have proved uniqueness.</details>

Let $a_0 < a_1 < a_2 \ldots$ be an infinite sequence of positive integers. Prove that there exists a unique integer $n\geq 1$ such that \[a_n < \frac{a_0+a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_n}{n} \leq a_{n+1}.\]
**Key Lemma:** If $S_i=S_{i-1}+u_i$ is a *cumulative sequence* with $S_0=0$ and $u_i>0$ for all $i$ , then for every positive integer $k$ , there is a unique positive integer $n$ so that, $S_n < k\leq S_{n+1}$ . *Proof:* Almost obvious. <details><summary>Solution</summary>Define the function  $f: \mathbb{Z}^+ \to \mathbb{Z}$  by \[f(k) = a_0 + a_1 + \ldots + a_{k-1} - (k-1)a_k.\] The condition  $a_n < \dfrac{a_0 + a_1 + \ldots + a_n}{n}$  simplifies to \[0 < a_0 + a_1 + \ldots + (n-1)a_n = f(n),\] and the condition  $\dfrac{a_0 + a_1 + \ldots + a_n}{n} \le a_{n+1}$  simplifies to \[a_0 + a_1 + \ldots + a_n - na_{n+1} = f(n+1) \le 0.\] Thus, we want to show that there is a unique positive integer  $n$  so that \[f(n+1) \le 0 < f(n).\] We claim that  $f$  is strictly decreasing over the positive integers: we have \[\begin{aligned} &\quad f(k+1) - f(k)  &= [a_0 + a_1 + \ldots + a_{k-1} + a_k - ka_{k+1}] - [a_0 + a_1 + \ldots + a_{k-1} - (k-1)a_k]  &= ka_k - ka_{k+1}  &= k(a_k - a_{k+1}) < 0 \end{aligned}\] since  $a_k < a_{k+1}$  for all  $k$ . Thus,  $f$  is strictly decreasing, as claimed. Further, since  $f(k)$  is always an integer, we must have  $f(k+1) \le f(k) - 1$  for all  $k$ .

Note that  $f(1) = a_0$ . Then, we have  $f(2) \le f(1) - 1 = a_0 - 1$ ,  $f(3) \le f(2) - 1 \le a_0 - 2$ , and by a straightforward induction argument,  $f(k) \le a_0 - (k-1)$  for all  $k \in \mathbb{Z}^+.$  Then \[f(a_0 + 1) \le a_0 - (a_0  + 1 - 1) = 0,\] so there is a positive integer  $m$  so that  $f(m) \le 0.$  Let  $m_0$  be the least positive integer  $m$  for which  $f(m) \le 0$ . Since  $f$  is strictly decreasing,  $f(k) \le 0$  if and only if  $k \ge m_0$ . Then, we must have  $f(m_0 - 1) > 0$ , so  $f(m_0) \le 0 < f(m_0 - 1).$  Thus,  $n = m_0 - 1$  is an integer satisfying the given conditions. Further, there cannot be another integer  $m_1 \neq m_0$  satisfying the given conditions. If there was such an  $m_1$ , then  $f(m_1) \le 0$ , so  $m_1 > m_0$ . However, then  $m_1 - 1 \ge m_0,$  so  $f(m_1 - 1) \le 0$ , a contradiction. Thus there is a unique positive  $n$  satisfying the given conditions.  $\square$</details>

First, note that  $a_1<a_0+a_1=\frac{a_0+a_1}{1}$ . Now, let  $k$  be the first number in the sequence such that  $a_k<\frac{a_0+a_1+...+a_k}{k}$  is not true (assuming that it exists). That means that  $a_k\geq\frac{a_0+a_1+...+a_k}{k}$ . A quick rearranging gives us  $a_k\geq\frac{a_0+a_1+...+a_{k-1}}{k-1}$ . Couple that with the fact that  $a_{k-1}<\frac{a_0+a_1+...+a_{k-1}}{k-1}$  and we have that  $n=k-1$  is a number satisfying the inequality at the beginning. Thus we must prove that  $k$  must exist and that for all  $m\geq{k}$ ,  $a_m\geq\frac{a_0+a_1+...+a_m}{m}$ . First, assume that for every  $n$ ,  $a_n<\frac{a_0+a_1+...+a_n}{n}$  then we can look at some specific number  $j$ . We know that  $a_j<\frac{a_0+a_1+...+a_j}{j}$ . We can rearrange to get  $(j-1)a_j<a_0+a_1+...+a_{j-1}$ . Now we add  $(j-1)(a_0+a_1+a_2+...+a_{j-1}$  on both sides:  $(j-1)(a_0+a_1+a_2+...+a_j)<j(a_0+a_1+a_2+...+a_{j-1}$  and we get  $\frac{a_0+a_1+a_2+...+a_j}{j}<\frac{a_0+a_1+a_2+...+a_{j-1}}{j-1}$ . Continuing with this process for  $j-1$ ,  $j-2$ , etc. we get  $a_j<\frac{a_0+a_1+a_2+...+a_j}{j}<\frac{a_0+a_1+a_2+...+a_{j-1}}{j-1}<\frac{a_0+a_1+a_2+...+a_{j-2}}{j-2}<...<\frac{a_0+a_1+a_2}{2}<a_0+a_1$ . Thus for all n in the sequence, we have  $a_n<a_0+a_1$  which is impossible because we have an infinite increasing sequence of integers. Thus, there is at least one  $n$  such that  $a_n\geq\frac{a_0+a_1+...+a_n}{n}$ . Once again let k be the first n to satisfy this. We'll start be showing that there is a  $N \geq 1$  such that  $\frac{a_0+a_1+\dots+a_N}{N} \leq a_{N+1}$ . Assume the contrary, in specific, \[ \frac{a_0+a_1+\dots+a_n}{n} > a_{n+1} \] for all  $n \geq 1$ . But then we also have \begin{align*} a_0+a_1+\dots+a_n &> na_{n+1} 
 & \geq (a_n+1)+(a_{n-1}+2)+\dots+(a_1+n) 
 &= (a_n+a_{n-1}+\dots+a_1)+(1+2+\dots+n) \end{align*} Thus   $a_0 > 1+2+\dots+n$  for all  $n \geq 1$ . But that's a contradiction, as  $a_0$  is a positive integer while  $1+2+\dots+n$  is not bounded.

Now we show that at least one such integer  $n$  exists. Assume the contrary. Then, for each positive integer  $n,$  one of the inequalities  $na_n\ge a_0+a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_n$  and  $na_{n+1}<a_0+a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_n$  must be satisfied. Consider an infinite sequence of positive integers a_0 < a_1 < a_2 < ... .**Step 1: Proving Existence**

Start by considering the integers 1, 2, ... , a_0. By the pigeonhole principle, at least one of these integers must appear in the sequence a_0, a_1, a_2, ... . Let a_k be the smallest integer among a_0, a_1, ... , a_k which is in {1, 2, ... , a_0}. Then, a_k >= 1.

Now, consider the average value of the first k terms: (a_0 + a_1 + ... + a_k) / k. If k = 1, then this average is a_0. If k > 1, then this average is greater than or equal to a_{k-1} (because the sequence is strictly increasing) and less than a_k (since the sum a_0 + a_1 + ... + a_k includes k terms, the largest of which is a_k).

Therefore, by the intermediate value theorem, there exists an integer n such that 1 <= n <= k and a_n < (a_0 + a_1 + ... + a_n) / n <= a_{n+1}.**Step 2: Proving Uniqueness**

Assume there exist two integers n and m (n < m) such that a_n < (a_0 + a_1 + ... + a_n) / n <= a_{n+1} and a_m < (a_0 + a_1 + ... + a_m) / m <= a_{m+1}.

Since n < m, we have a_n < (a_0 + a_1 + ... + a_n) / n <= (a_0 + a_1 + ... + a_m) / n <= (a_0 + a_1 + ... + a_m) / m <= a_{m+1}. But a_n is smaller than the average of the first n terms and greater than the average of the first m terms, which contradicts the ordering of the sequence.

Therefore, there can be only one such integer n.

Thus, there exists a unique integer n >= 1 such that a_n < (a_0 + a_1 + ... + a_n) / n <= a_{n+1}.

Therefore, the first time there is a positive integer  $j$  such that  $c_{j} \ge b_{j}$ , then all the integers  $m$  greater than  $j$  also satisfy  $c_{m} \ge b_{m}$ . So, it suffices to show that such an integer  $n$  exists because at most one integer can satisfy  $c_{n} < b_{n}$  and  $c_{n+1} \ge b_{n+1}$ .

We now just need to show that there is at least one number  $l$  such that  $c_{l} \ge b_{l}$ . FTSOC, suppose otherwise. Then, since  $c_{1} = 0$  and  $b_{1} = a_{0}$ ,  $c_{1} < b_{1}$ . However, note that the difference between  $c_{i}$  and  $b_{i}$  is a monovariant as as  $i$  decreases, the difference between them decreases by at least  $1$ . Hence, when  $l$  is  $a_{0}$ , the difference will be  $\le 0$ , which is a contradiction.

Thus we are done

Start with  $n=1$ . Clearly  $a_1 < a_0+a_1$ . If  $a_0+a_1 \le a_2$ , then  $a_2 \ge \frac{a_0+a_1+a_2}{2}$  so  $a_3 > a_2 \ge \frac{a_0+a_1+a_2}{2}$  so  $a_3 > \frac{a_0+a_1+a_2+a_3}{3}$  and in general  $a_{n} > \frac{a_0+\ldots + a_n}{n}$ , implying uniqueness. Otherwise,  $a_2 < a_0+a_1$  so  $a_2 < \frac{a_0+a_1+a_2}{2}$ . Induction upward finishes.

Write \( a_k = a_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} b_i \) for \( b_i \geq 1 \). The desired inequality is equivalent to
\[
b_2 + 2b_3 + \cdots + (n-1)b_n < a_0 \leq b_2 + 2b_3 + \cdots + (n-1)b_n + nb_{n+1}.
\]
It remains to observe that the sequence \( c_n = b_2 + 2b_3 + \cdots + (n-1)b_n \) grows unbounded as \( n \) increases (since \( c_{n+1} - c_n = nb_{n+1} \geq n \geq 1 \)) and that \( c_1 = 0 < a_0 \). Therefore, \( a_0 \) is located between some two consecutive terms of the sequence \( c_n \) and we are done.

**Claim:** $n$ is unique *Proof.* Suppose an $n$ does work, let $r$ be the smallest $n$ that works. Assume $b > r$ also works. From here denote \[ S_k = a_0 + a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_k. \] Note we have \[ b a_b < S_b \leq r a_{r+1} + \sum_{i=r+1}^b a_i \leq r a_b + (b-r)a_b = b a_b, \] or \[ b a_b < b a_b, \]absurd. **Claim:**An $n$ exists. *Proof.*Suppose FTSOC no $n$ exists. We claim that \[ S_k > k \, a_{k+1} \quad \text{for all } k \geq 1 \] and proceed by induction. **Base Case:** $k=1$ is true since $S_1 > a_2$ . $n=1$ gives $a_1 < (a_0+a_1)$ , which is true, thus $a_0+a_1 > a_2$ for no such $n$ to exist. **Inductive Step:**For $k+1$ , by inductive hypothesis, \[ \frac{S_k + a_{k+1}}{k+1} > \frac{S_k}{k} > a_{k+1}, \] so \[ \frac{S_{k+1}}{k+1} > a_{k+2} \] for $n$ to be nonexistent, and our induction is complete. **SubClaim:** As $k=n \to \infty$ \[S_n \leq n a_{n+1}\] must occur. *Proof.*FTSOC assume that \[ S_k > k a_{k+1} \quad \text{for all } k. \] Compare how the two sides change when passing the index from $k$ to $k+1$ : The left side increases by \[ S_{k+1} - S_k = a_{k+1}. \] The right side increases by \[ (k+1)a_{k+2} - k a_{k+1} = a_{k+1} + (k+1)(a_{k+2} - a_{k+1}). \] Since $a_{k+2} > a_{k+1}$ and they are integers, we have \[ (k+1)a_{k+2} - k a_{k+1} \geq a_{k+1} + (k+1). \] Thus, at each step, the right-hand side grows at least $(k+1)$ more than the left-hand side. If initially $S_k > k a_{k+1}$ , then after finitely many steps the faster-growing RHS will overtake the LHS, absurd. Thus an $n$ must exist and be unique so we are done.

Note that for all  $k\geq 1$ , either  $a_k<\frac{a_0+\cdots+a_k}{k}$  (1) or  $a_k\geq\frac{a_0+\cdots+a_{k-1}}{k-1}$  (2).  $k=1$  satisfies (1). Also, (2) is equivalent to  $(k-1)a_k-a_0-\cdots-a_{k-1}\geq 0$ . Since  $(k-1)a_k-a_0-\cdots-a_{k-1}\geq (k-1)-a_0$ , all sufficiently large  $k$  satisfy (2). Thus we may take  $n$  maximal satisfying (1) and this will satisfy the condition. If  $k$  satisfies (2) and  $k+1$  satisfies (1), then  $ka_{k+1}< a_0+\cdots+a_k\leq ka_k$ , a contradiction. Thus all  $k>n$  satisfy (2) so  $n$  is unique.  $\square$

Nice problem. We will solve the problem in two stages, we will first show there exists such \(n\) and then prove it is unique.

Assume on contary that there does not exist such \(n\). Let us call \(a_n < \frac{a_0+a_1 + \ldots + a_n}{n}\) part as LHS-part for \(n\) and \(\frac{a_0+a_1 + \ldots + a_n}{n} \leq a_{n+1} \) part as RHS-part for \(n\) for convenience. Observe that if RHS-part for \(n\) is true, then LHS-part for \(n+1\) is false and vice-versa. For \(n=1\) it is trivial that LHS-part is true which implies inductively that RHS-part is false for all \(n\). So we get the following inequalities:
\[
a_0 + a_1 > a_2
\]\[
a_0 + a_1+a_2 > 2a_3
\]\[
a_0 + a_1+a_2+a_3 > 3a_4
\]\[
\ldots
\]\[
a_0 + a_1 + \ldots +a_n > na_{n+1}
\]
If we sum up the ineqaulites we get \(n(a_0+a_1) + (n-1)a_2 +(n-2)a_3 + \ldots +2a_{n-1} + a_n\) \(>\) \(na_{n+1} + (n-1)a_n + \ldots +2a_3 + a_2\) \(>\) \(na_{n+1} +1a_n + 2a_{n-1} + \ldots + (n-1)a_2\) which implies \(a_0 +a_1 > a_n\) for all \(n \geq 2\) which is a contraction since \(a_n\) is increasing hence unbouned. So we successfully proved that there exists such \(n\). Now let's prove it's uniqueness.

Observe that both RHS-part and LHS-part can't be false for any \(n\) as it would imply \(a_n \geq \frac{a_0 + a_1 + \ldots + a_n}{n} > a_{n+1}\) which is a contradiction since the sequence is in increasing order. Let \(n=k\) be the smallest number to satisfy the ineqaulity. Which means both RHS-part and LHS-part for \(k\) is true. This implies LHS-part for \(k+1\) is false. As both parts can't be false we get RHS-part for \(k+1\) is true which implies LHS-part for \(k+2\) is false. Continuing this pattern it is easy to see that no \(n\) satisfy both ineqaulities other then \(k\). Hence the problem is completed. \( \square \)

Let  $P$  and  $Q$  be on segment  $BC$  of an acute triangle  $ABC$  such that  $\angle PAB=\angle BCA$  and  $\angle CAQ=\angle ABC$ . Let  $M$  and  $N$  be the points on  $AP$  and  $AQ$ , respectively, such that  $P$  is the midpoint of  $AM$  and  $Q$  is the midpoint of  $AN$ . Prove that the intersection of  $BM$  and  $CN$  is on the circumference of triangle  $ABC$ .

*Proposed by Giorgi Arabidze, Georgia.*
solution_md:
<details><summary>synthetic sol</summary>$\angle APQ=\angle AQP=\angle A\implies \Delta APQ$  is isosceles
Let  $T=BM\cap CN, A'$  be the reflection of  $A$  by  $PQ$ , and  $K$  be the midpoint of  $BC$ Note that there exists a homothety of centre  $A$  and ratio  $2$  that takes  $P,Q$  to  $M,N$ , furthermore, it takes the feet of the  $A$ -perpendicular to  $A'$ , therefore,  $A'$  is the midpoint of  $MN$ . 
We also have, by that homothety, that  $QP// MN\implies BC//MN\implies \Delta MTN\sim \Delta BTC\implies T$  is the centre of a spiral similarity that takes  $MN$  to  $BC\implies$  this similarity also takes  $A'$  to  $K\implies A',T,K$  are collinear.

Therefore, let  $T'$  be the reflection of  $T$  by  $BC$ . By reflecting  $\overline{A'TK}$  by  $BC$ , we have that  $A-T'-K\implies T'$  lies on the  $A$ -midline, therefore, it is sufficient to show that  $T$  lies on the  $A$ -symmedian (one can prove this by moving a point  $P$  across the  $A$ -symmedian an checking that the only point where its reflection by  $BC$  lies on the  $A$ -midline is when  $P$  also lies on the circumcircle).

Let  $l_1,l_2$  be the tangents to  $(ABC)$  at  $B$  and  $C$ . Note that  $\angle PAB=\angle C=\angle(l_1,BC)\implies l_1//AP$ , similarly, we have that  $l_2//AQ\implies l_1\cap l_2\in AT$ . However, it is well-known that  $l_1\cap l_2$  lies on the  $A$ -symmedian, therefore,  $T$  lies on the  $A$ -symmedian $\implies$   $T$  is the 2nd intersection of the  $A$ -symmedian with  $(ABC)$ .</details>
<details><summary>bary sol</summary>Apply bary wrt  $\Delta ABC$    $$ \Delta ABC\sim\Delta PBA\sim\Delta QAC\implies PB=\frac{c^2}{a}, QC=\frac{b^2}{a}\implies P=(0:a^2-c^2:c^2), Q=(0:b^2:a^2-b^2) $$    $$ \vec{M}=2\vec{P}-\vec{A}=\left(-1,\frac{2a^2-2c^2}{a^2},\frac{2c^2}{a^2}\right)=\left(-\frac{a^2}{2}:a^2-c^2:c^2\right), N=\left(-\frac{a^2}{2}:b^2:a^2-b^2\right) $$  By letting  $T=BM\cap CN$ , we have that  $T-B-M\implies T=(-a^2:t:2c^2)$ ,  $T-C-N\implies T=(-a^2:2b^2:t')\implies T=(-a^2:2b^2:2c^2)$ Now, it is easy to check that  $a^2yz+b^2xz+c^2xy=0\implies T\in (ABC)$</details>
<details><summary>complex sol</summary>Complex bash with  $(ABC)$  as the unit circle
Let  $T$  be the  $2$ -nd intersection of the  $A$ -symmedian with  $(ABC)$ , and  $A'$  be the reflection of  $A$  by  $BC$ . Finally, let  $l$  be the line parallel to  $BC$  that passes through  $A'$ .
We have that   $$ \frac{\frac{2bc}{b+c}-t}{a-t}=\frac{\frac{2}{b+c}-\frac1{t}}{\frac1{a}-\frac1{t}}=\frac{\frac{2at}{b+c}-a}{t-a}\implies t(2a-b-c)=ab+ac-2bc\implies t=-\frac{2bc-ac-ab}{2a-b-c} $$  Redefine  $M=BT\cap l$  and  $N=CT\cap l$ .   $$ A'M//BC\iff m-\frac{ab+ac-bc}{a}=-a+b+c-\overline{m}bc\iff \overline{m}=\frac{-a^2+2ab+2ac-bc-am}{abc} $$    $$ B-T-M\iff \overline{m}=\frac{b+t-m}{bt}=\frac{-a^2+2ab+2ac-bc-am}{abc}\iff\boxed{m=\frac{t(-a^2+2ab+ac-bc)-abc}{a(t-c)},\ n=\frac{t(-a^2+2bc+ab-bc)-abc}{a(t-b)}} $$  Now, let  $P',Q'$  be the midpoints of  $AM$  and  $AN$ .   $$ \boxed{p'=\frac{a+m}{2}=\frac{t(2ab+ac-bc)-ac(b+1)}{2a(t-c)}, q'=\frac{t(2ac+ab-bc)-ab(c+1)}{2a(t-b)}} $$  Now, it is easy to check that  $\overline{p'}=\frac{b+c-p'}{bc}, \overline{q'}=\frac{b+c-q'}{bc}\implies B-Q-P-C$  and that  $\frac{p'-a}{b-a}\div \frac{b-c}{a-c}, \frac{q'-a}{c-a}\div \frac{c-b}{a-b}\in\mathbb{R}\implies \measuredangle PAB=\measuredangle CAQ\implies P'=P, Q'=Q$ , so we're done!</details>

$QP$  and  $NM$  are parallel. $\angle{ANM} = \angle{AQC} = \angle{A}$  $\angle{AMN} = \angle{APB} = \angle{A}$ Let  $R$  be the intersection of  $BM$  and  $CN$ .
Let  $X, Y$  be points on  $AB, AC$  such that  $A$  is the midpoint of  $BX$  and  $A$  is the midpoint of  $YC$  $\triangle{ABC}$  and  $\triangle{QAC}$  are similar, then  $\triangle{XBC}$  and  $\triangle{NAC}$  are similar. Then  $\angle{ANC} = \angle{BXC}$   $\triangle{ACB}$  and  $\triangle{PAB}$  are similar, then  $\triangle{YCB}$  and  $\triangle{MAB}$  are similar. Then  $\angle{A} = \angle{BXC} + \angle{CYB}$   $\angle{RNM} = \angle{ANM} - \angle{ANC} = \angle{A} - \angle{BXC}$  $\angle{RMN} = \angle{RMN} - \angle{AMB} = \angle{A} - \angle{CYB}$  $\angle{RNM} + \angle{RMN} = 2\angle{A} - \angle{BXC} - \angle{CYB} = \angle{A}$  $\angle{BRC} + \angle{A} = 180$

Let  $x=<QCN$  and  $y=<PBM$ , by similitude we have  $\frac{AQ}{AB}=\frac{AC}{BC}=\frac{QC}{AC}$  so  $QN=\frac{AB.AC}{BC}$  and  $QC=\frac{AC^2}{BC}$  and  $<CQN=180-<AQC=180-A$  so in the triangle  $QCN$  we have \[\frac{\sin(x-A)}{\sin(x)}=\frac{AC}{AB}\] and by the same way \[\frac{\sin(y-A)}{\sin(y)}=\frac{AB}{AC}\]
so \[\sin(x-A)\sin(y-A)=\sin(x)\sin(y)\] so  $-\cos(x+y-2A)+\cos(x-y)=2\sin(x)\sin(y)$  and therefore \[\cos(x+y-2A)=\cos(x+y)\] which gives \[x+y=A\] and if  $R$  is the intersection point \[<BRC+<BCR=A\]

Barycentric coordinates overkill this problem, yet straightfoward and not messy, took me about 5 minutes.
We have similar triangles  $PBA$ ,  $QAC$ ,  $ABC$ , with area ratios  $\frac{c^2}{a^2}, \frac{b^2}{a^2}, 1$  respectively.
Therefore we have the barycentric coordinates  $P=(0:1-\frac{c^2}{a^2}:\frac{c^2}{a^2}), Q=(0:\frac{b^2}{a^2}:1-\frac{b^2}{a^2}).$ Now note that the area of  $MAB$  is the double of  $PAB$ , and area of  $MCA$  is the double of  $PCA$ .  $MBC$  has the same area as  $ABC$ , but negative, and do the similar for point  $N$ .
One then obtains  $M=(-1:2(1-\frac{c^2}{a^2}):\frac{2c^2}{a^2}), N=(-1:\frac{2b^2}{a^2}:2(1-\frac{c^2}{a^2})).$ Lines  $BM$  and  $CN$  have equations  $z=-\frac{2c^2x}{a^2}$  and  $y=-\frac{2b^2x}{a^2}$  respectively.
The intersection point has un-homogenized coordinates  $(1:-\frac{2b^2x}{a^2}:-\frac{2c^2x}{a^2})$ , which can be easily verified to satisfy the circumcircle equation  $a^2yz+b^2xz+c^2xy=0$ .

Yay!

Another approach.

Let  $ O $  be the circumcenter of  $ \triangle ABC $ . Observe that  $ OB \perp AP $ ,  $ OC \perp AQ $ . Let  $ OB \cap AP = L $ ,  $ OC \cap AQ = K $ .

Let  $ X,Y $  be the midpoints of  $ AB,AC $ . Let  $ XP \cap YQ = S $ . Then, we want to show that  $ S $  lies on circle  $ (AXY) $ , i.e, the circle  $ \Gamma $  with diameter  $ OA $ .

Note that  $ X,K,L,Y $  lie on  $ \Gamma $ , so by Pascal's Theorem on  $ KOLYAX $ , we get  $ KO \cap YA = C, LO \cap XA = B $  and  $ LY \cap KX := D $  are collinear, i.e  $ D $  is on  $ \overline{BC} = \overline{PQ} $ . Considering the hexagon  $ KALYSX $ , we have the intersections,  $ KA \cap SY = Q, LA \cap SX = P $  and  $ LY \cap KX = D $  are collinear, so by converse of Pascal's Theorem,  $ S $  is on the unique conic passing through  $ A,K,L,X,Y $  which is precisely circle  $ \Gamma $ .

Let  $X$  and  $Y$  be the midpoints of  $AB$  and  $AC$ , respectively, and let  $Z$  be the intersection between  $PX$  and  $QY$ . Also, let  $ \gamma = \angle ACB $  and  $\beta = \angle ABC$ . A quick angle chasing show us that  $\angle APQ = \angle AQP = 180 -\alpha -\beta$ , and the triangles  $ABP$  and  $CAQ$  are similar, where we get  $\angle YQC = \angle APX = \alpha$  (because both  $QY$  and  $PX$  are medians of the same corresponding size). Thus,  $\angle YPQ=180- \alpha - \beta - \gamma$  and finally:  $\angle XZY = \angle QZP = 180 - \angle ZQP - \angle ZPQ = 180 -\alpha - (180 - \alpha - \beta - \gamma)= \beta + \gamma = 180 - \angle A$ .

So  $AXZY$  is cyclic.

Now, let  $R$  be the intersection of  $BM$  and  $CN$ . A homotety of center  $A$  and ratio 2 takes  $X$  to  $B$ ,  $Y$  to  $C$ ,  $Q$  to  $N$  and  $P$  to  $M$ . So it takes  $Z$  to  $R$ , which means that  $ABRC$  is cyclic as well. This ends the proof.

It's very nice and easy problem.Let  $ (BAQ) \cap (CAP) = X $ , and let  $ AX \cap (ABC)=Y $ ,  $ BM \cap CN=Y $ .We have by angles chasing  $ AQ=AP $  ,  $ MY || PX $  and  $ NY || QX $  so the triangles  $ QXP $  and  $ NYM $  are similar hamotetic (with ratio 2) .On the other  $ \angle NYM = \angle QXP=180 - \angle BAC $  so we have  $ Y $  lies on the circumcircle of the triangle  $ ABC $ . What an excellent barycentric tutorial problem!

Since  $PB = c^2/a$  we have  $P = (0 : a^2-c^2 : c^2)$ , so  $M = (-a^2 : {-} : 2c^2)$ . Similarly  $N = (-a^2 : 2b^2 : {-})$ . Thus  $\overline{BM} \cap \overline{CN}$  is  $(-a^2 : 2b^2 : 2c^2)$  which clearly lies on the circumcircle.

A good and easy IMO problem. I saw the cyclic quadrilateral and then the proof is already done. There are many different ways of approaching the problem. A purely analytical solution might be doable but gory.

Let  $BM$  and  $CN$  meet at  $J.$  From similar triangles  $\triangle ABP$  and  $\triangle ACQ,$  we have  $\dfrac{AP}{BP} = \dfrac{AQ}{QC} \implies \dfrac{PM}{BP} = \dfrac{QM}{QC}.$  Combined with the fact that  $\angle BPM = \angle ABC + \angle BCA = \angle QCN,$  we deduce that  $\triangle BPM \sim \triangle QCN,$  implying  $\angle PBM = \angle QCN.$  Let  $\angle PBM = \angle QCN = \theta.$   

Again, from  $\triangle ABP \sim \triangle ACQ,$   $\dfrac{PM}{BM} = \dfrac{AP}{BP}= \dfrac{AB}{AC}.$  We have that  $\angle BPM = \angle ABC + \angle BCA = 180^{\circ} - \angle BAC.$  We then have  $\angle BMP = \theta - \angle BAC .$  Similarly,  $\angle CNQ =\theta - \angle BAC.$  From sine rule in  $\triangle BPM,$   $\dfrac{PM}{\sin \theta} = \dfrac{BP}{\sin (\theta  - \angle BAC)}$  and from sine rule in  $\triangle CQN,$   $\dfrac{QN}{\sin \theta } = \dfrac{QC}{\sin (\theta - \angle BAC  )}.$  Combining them, we see that
\[\sin^2(\theta - \angle BAC) = \sin^2 \theta \implies \cos (2(\theta - \angle BAC)) + 1 = \cos^2 \theta   \implies 2 \theta = \angle BAC \implies \theta = \dfrac{\angle BAC}{2}.\]
Let  $BM$  and  $CN$  meet at  $J.$  From isoceles  $\triangle JBC,$  we have that  $\angle BJC = 180^{\circ} - 2 \theta = 180^{\circ} - \angle BAC,$  so  $(ABJC)$  is cyclic, as desired.  $\blacksquare$

Let $P$ and $Q$ be on segment $BC$ of an acute triangle $ABC$ such that $\angle PAB=\angle BCA$ and $\angle CAQ=\angle ABC$ . Let $M$ and $N$ be the points on $AP$ and $AQ$ , respectively, such that $P$ is the midpoint of $AM$ and $Q$ is the midpoint of $AN$ . Prove that the intersection of $BM$ and $CN$ is on the circumference of triangle $ABC$ .
My solution : First of all, we notice that $\triangle{CPA} \sim \triangle{CAB}$ and $\triangle{BAQ} \sim \triangle{BCA}$ , so $\angle{QPA} = \angle{BAC} = \angle{PQA}$ hence, $\triangle{APQ}$ is isosceles. So, $\angle{BPM} = \angle{CPA} = \angle{BAC}$ . This also means $PA = PM = QA = QN$ . Clearly, from $PQ \parallel MN$ , we get $\angle{AMN} = \angle{APQ} = \angle{BAC}$ Suppose that $X$ is the intersection of $BN$ and $CM$ , then we need to prove $\angle{BXM} = \angle{BAC} = \angle{BPM}$ or this means it suffices to prove that $MXPB$ is cyclic and again this implies that we only need to prove that $CP\cdot CB = CX\cdot CM = CA^2$ . Now, i will use length chasing to prove $CX\cdot CM = CA^2$ . Denote by $a, b, c$ the length of the sides $BC, CA, AB$ respectively. Then, because $\triangle{CPA} \sim \triangle{CAB}$ we have $\frac{AP}{AC} = \frac{BA}{BC}$ so $AP = \frac{bc}{a}$ . Now, we compute some length, that is : \[\frac{\frac{MN}{2}}{MA} = \cos \angle{AMN} = \cos \angle{A} = \frac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc}\] \[\frac{MN}{2} = \frac{2bc}{a}\cdot\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc}\] \[MN = \frac{2b^2+2c^2-2a^2}{a}\] We also have by the law of cosine in $AMC$ : \[CM^2 = AM^2 + AC^2 - 2\cdot AM\cdot AC\cdot\cos{\angle{MAC}}\] \[CM^2 = AM^2 + AC^2 - 2\cdot AM\cdot AC\cdot\cos{\angle{B}}\] But, $\cos{\angle{B}} = \frac{c^2 + a^2 - b^2}{2bc}$ . Very low power solution using the most basic of geometry tools: cyclic quadrilaterals, collinear points, and similar triangles. 

Denote by T the intersection of circles APC and AQB, X the intersection point of the tangents at B and C to the circucmricle of ABC, K the intersection of AX with the circumcircle of ABC, and R the intersection of BK with AP.
1. Let <BAT = <ACT (given) = x, <CAT = <ABT (given) = y. 
2. Angle chase to get BTC = 2A and ATB = ATC = 180-A. 
3. Angle chase to get BOC = 2A, BXC = 180-2A, <XBC = <XCB = A so BTOCX is cyclic. 
4. <OTK = <OTX = <OBX = 90 (3)
5. <ATB + <BTX = 180-A + BCX = 180 so A, T, X are collinear. 
6. A, T, K, X are collinear by definition of K. 
7. <APC = <PBA + <BAP = B + x + <TAP = B + x + TCP = B + x + C-x = B + C (angle chase + ATPC is cyclic by definition of P)
8. <ARB = x (angle chase)
9. <APT = <ACT = x (ATPC is cyclic by definition of P)
10. <TAP = <KAR, <APT = <ARK (=ARB) so triangle TAM is similar to triangle KAR. 
11. RM/RA = KT/TA
12. KT/TA = 1/2 (4)

14. PM/PA = 1/2 (by definition of P)
15. P=R (Both P and R lie on the same line, on the same side of P, and satisfy the same length ratios)
16. Line BP = BR passes through K by definition of R 
17. Similarly CQ passes through K
18. BP and CQ intersect at K, which by definition lies on the circumcircle of ABC

We make an inversion with center  $A$  and an arbitrary radius  $r$ . We use the notation  $X'$  to denote the inverse of a point  $X$ .
Since  $B,Q,P,C$  are collinear, the points  $A,B',Q',P',C'$  are concyclic. Also,  $AB$  tangent to  $\odot APC$  implies  $AB' \parallel P'C'$ ; and  $AC$  tangent to  $\odot ABQ$  implies  $AC' \parallel B'Q'$ . Hence  $AB'P'C'$  y  $AC'Q'B'$  are trapezoids, and since they are cyclic, they are isosceles trapezoids.
Since  $P$  and  $Q$  were the midpoints of  $AM$  and  $AN$  respectively, it follows that  $M'$  and  $N'$  are the midpoints of  $AP'$  and  $AQ'$ .
We want to prove that  $BM \cap CN \in \odot ABC$ . This is equivalent to proving that  $\odot AB'M' \cap \odot AC'N' \in B'C'$ . Now, by symmetry, the circle  $\odot AB'M'$  passes through the midpoint of the other diagonal of the isosceles trapezoid  $AB'P'C'$ , that is  $B'C'$ . Analogously,  $\odot AC'N'$  passes through the midpoint of  $B'C'$ . So  $\odot AB'M'$  and  $\odot AC'N'$  meet over  $B'C'$ , and the problem follows.  $\blacksquare$

Let  $X=BM\cap CN$ , and define  $B'=AB\cap MN$ ,  $C'=AC\cap MN$ .  First note that the condition  $\angle PAB=\angle BCA$  implies  $\triangle PAB\sim\triangle ACB$ , and likewise  $\angle QAC=\angle CBA$  implies  $\triangle CAQ\sim\triangle CBA$ .  Therefore  $\angle PQA=\angle BAC=\angle APQ$  and  $\triangle APQ$  is isosceles.

Next note that a homothety centered at  $A$  with scale factor  $2$  send  $\triangle ABC$  to  $\triangle AB'C'$  (due to the fact that it sends  $\triangle APQ$  to  $\triangle AMN$ ), so additionally  $\triangle ACQ\sim\triangle AC'N$ , etc.  Length "bashing" gives \[\dfrac{AB}{AM}=\dfrac{AB}{2AP}=\dfrac{CA}{2CQ}=\dfrac{C'A}{2C'N}=\dfrac{C'C}{C'N},\] which coupled with  $\angle PAB=\angle AC'N$  gives  $\triangle BAM\sim\triangle CC'N\implies \angle XMA=\angle XNM$ .  Similarly,  $\angle XMN=\angle XNA$ .  Therefore \begin{align*}\angle BXC&=\pi-(\angle XNM+\angle XMN)=\pi-\dfrac12(\angle ANM+\angle AMN)&=\pi-\dfrac12(\angle BAC+\angle BAC)=\pi-\angle BAC,\end{align*} establishing the desired cyclicity.   $\blacksquare$

The idea of the proof is to prove that the points  $B,N,X,Q$  are con-cyclic. We do that by computing  $CQ \cdot CB$  and  $CX \cdot CN$ . Their equality implies the desired result.

This involves the computation of several distances namely :
 
The letters  $a,b,c$  designate the original triangle sides. $BQ=a-\frac{b^2}{a}$  $BP=\frac{c^2}{a}$  $CQ=\frac{b^2}{a}$  $CP=a-\frac{c^2}{a}$  $AQ=AP=QN=PM= \frac{bc}{a}$ All of these can be clearly seen as true because of the similarity between  $ABC,AQC,APB$ . $BN=\sqrt{2(a^2-2b^2+\frac{b^4}{a^2}+\frac{b^2c^2}{a^2})-c^2}$  $NC=\sqrt{2(\frac{b^4}{a^2}+\frac{b^2c^2}{a^2})-b^2}$  $CM=\sqrt{2(a^2-2c^2+\frac{c^4}{a^2}+\frac{b^2c^2}{a^2})-b^2}$  $BM=\sqrt{2(\frac{c^4}{a^2}+\frac{b^2c^2}{a^2})-c^2}$ These can be seen as true because of [http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollonius%27_theorem](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollonius%27_theorem).

Using these we can determine that  $CX= \sqrt{2(\frac{b^4}{a^2}+\frac{b^2c^2}{a^2})-b^2} \cdot \frac{a^2}{2b^2+2c^2-a^2}$ Using this we can verify that the above quantities are indeed the same and equal  $b^2$ .

First,  $\triangle{ACQ} \sim \triangle{ABC} \sim \triangle{ABP}$  imply  $CQ = AC^2/BC$  and  $BP = AB^2/BC$ . Place  $ABC$  on the unit circle and assign coordinates  $A=(a,\sqrt{1-a^2}),B=(t,-\sqrt{1-t^2}),C=(-t,-\sqrt{1-t^2})$  (we put  $BC$  below the  $x$ -axis for  $ABC$  to be acute). To save some computational work, we'll now set  $m = (\sqrt{1-a^2} + \sqrt{1-t^2})^2$ . Computing lengths, we have   $$ CQ = \frac{(a+t)^2 + m}{2t}, BP = \frac{(a-t)^2 + m}{2t}. $$   We can find coordinates   $$ P = \left(\frac{-a^2+2at+t^2-m}{2t}, -\sqrt{1-t^2}\right), Q = \left(\frac{a^2+2at-t^2+m}{2t}, -\sqrt{1-t^2}\right). $$   Using the midpoint formula, we can obtain coordinates   $$ M = \left(\frac{-a^2 + at + t^2 - m}{t}, -2\sqrt{1-t^2} - \sqrt{1-a^2}\right), N = \left(\frac{a^2 + at - t^2 + m}{t}, -2\sqrt{1-t^2} - \sqrt{1-a^2}\right). $$   The equations of lines  $BM$  and  $CN$  respectively are   $$ y + \sqrt{1-t^2} = \frac{\sqrt{m}}{a^2-at+m}(x-t)t, y + \sqrt{1-t^2} = \frac{\sqrt{m}}{-a^2-at-m}(x+t)t. $$   Setting the RHS of both equations equal and cross-multiplying, we have   $$ (-a^2 - at - m)x + (a^2 + at + m)t = (a^2 - at + m)x + (a^2 - at + m)t. $$   So then the  $x$ -coordinate of  $BM \cap CN$  is  $x = \frac{at^2}{a^2+m}$ . Plugging this  $x$  into the equation for  $BM$ , the  $y$ -coordinate coincidentally simplifies down to  $y = \frac{-t^2\sqrt{m}}{a^2+m} - \sqrt{1-t^2}.$  Our final task is to show that  $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ . We have   $$ x^2 + y^2 = \frac{a^2t^4}{(a^2+m)^2} + \frac{mt^4}{(a^2+m)^2}+\frac{2t^2\sqrt{m(1-t^2)}}{a^2+m}+1-t^2 $$     $$ = \frac{t^4}{a^2+m}+\frac{2t^2(1-t^2) + 2t^2\sqrt{1-t^2}\sqrt{1-a^2}}{a^2+m} + 1-t^2. $$  Note that   $$ 2t^2 - t^4 + 2t^2\sqrt{1-t^2}\sqrt{1-a^2} = t^2(a^2 + 2 - t^2 - a^2 + 2\sqrt{1-t^2}\sqrt{1-a^2}) = t^2(a^2 + m). $$   What we have for  $x^2 + y^2$  miraculously simplifies to  $1$ .

Firstly from the angle condition, it is obvious that $AB$ and $AC$ are respectively tangent to $\odot(ACP)$ and $\odot(ABQ)$ . Now, let $T$ be the point of intersection of the $A- \text{symmedian}$ wrt $\triangle ABC$ with $\odot(ABC)$ and $S$ be the midpoint of $\overline{AT}$ . Now, notice that by midline theorem, $SQ \parallel TN$ and $SP \parallel TM$ . Also, notice that $S$ is the center of spiral similarity taking $BA \mapsto AC$ . Finally we have : $$ \angle QAS = \angle BAS - \angle BAQ = \angle BAC - \angle SAC - (\angle BAC - \angle QAC) = [ \alpha - \beta + \angle SBC] - [\alpha - \beta] = \angle SBC = \angle SBQ \iff ABQS = \text{cyclic} $$ Similarly $ASPC$ is cyclic. Thus we get $\angle TSQ = \angle CBA = \angle CTA \iff CT \parallel QS \iff T \in \overline{CN}$ . Similarly, $T \in \overline{BM}$ . So, in other words we have $\overline{BM} \cap \overline {CN} = T \in \odot(ABC) \blacksquare$

stem_md: For each positive integer  $n$ , the Bank of Cape Town issues coins of denomination  $\frac1n$ . Given a finite collection of such coins (of not necessarily different denominations) with total value at most most  $99+\frac12$ , prove that it is possible to split this collection into  $100$  or fewer groups, such that each group has total value at most  $1$ .
solution_md:
I will prove the desired result for when the total value of the coins is at most  $k-\tfrac{1}{2}$  and we wish to split the collection into  $k$  or fewer groups, where  $k$  is a positive integer. The given problem is the case when  $k=100.$  

I proceed by induction on  $k.$  

For the base case, it is obvious that if the total value of the coins is at most  $\tfrac{1}{2}$  and we wish to split the collection into  $1$  or fewer groups, then we can just put all of our coins into a single group. 

Now, suppose that the desired result holds true for some  $k=i$  where  $i$  is a positive integer. We wish to show that it then must hold true for  $k=i+1.$  

If there is a coin of denomination  $1$  in the collection, then we can put the coin in its own group, and then the sum of the remaining coins will be  $i-\tfrac{1}{2}.$  By the inductive hypothesis, this remaining collection can be split into  $i$  or fewer groups such that each group has total value at most  $1,$  so it results that the original collection can be split into  $i+1$  or fewer such groups. 

Otherwise, let us perform the following algorithm:
[list=1]
    [*] If there exist two coins with denominations both equal to  $\tfrac{1}{2j}$  for some positive integer  $j,$  then let us temporarily ``merge" the coins, i.e. we will put them into groups in pairs. Let us perform this operation repeatedly until it cannot be done any more.
    [*] Next, if there are  $j$  coins with denominations all equal to  $\tfrac{1}{j}$  for some positive integer  $j,$  then let us temporarily merge all of these coins. Let us perform this operation repeatedly until it cannot be done any more.
    [*] Now, let us put all coins of denomination  $1$  and  $\tfrac{1}{2}$  in the first group, all coins of denomination  $\tfrac{1}{3}$  and  $\tfrac{1}{4}$  in the second group, and so on, until we put all coins of denomination  $\tfrac{1}{2i+1}$  and  $\tfrac{1}{2i+2}$  into the  $(i+1)$ th group.
    [*] If we have a coin of denomination  $\tfrac{1}{j}$  for  $j>2i+2,$  then place that coin into a group currently with sum at most  $1-\tfrac{1}{j}.$  Let us perform this operation repeatedly until it cannot be done any more.
    [*] Finally, un-merge all of the merged groups.
[/list]
Observe that the first and second steps of this algorithm ensure that for all  $i \ge 0,$  there is at most one (unmerged) coin of denomination  $\tfrac{1}{2i+2}$  left, and for all  $i \ge 1,$  there are at most  $2i+1$  (unmerged) coins of denomination  $\tfrac{1}{2i+1}.$  Therefore, since
\begin{align*}
    \frac{2i}{2i+1}+\frac{1}{2i+2} &<\frac{2i}{2i+1}+\frac{1}{2i+1} 
    &= 1,
\end{align*}
the third step in the algorithm always creates valid groups. 

Next, since the total value of the coins is at most  $i+\tfrac{1}{2},$  we know that the expected amount of space left in a group after some portion of the coins have already been placed is at least   $$ \frac{\tfrac{1}{2}}{i+1}=\frac{1}{2i+2}. $$   Therefore, there is always some space left with size greater than or equal to  $\tfrac{1}{2i+2},$  implying that all coins of denomination  $\tfrac{1}{j}$  for  $j>2i+2$  can be validly placed into the groups in the fourth step of the algorithm. 

Finally, the fifth step of the algorithm brings us back to the given coin collection, so having verified that all steps can be performed, we know that the stated algorithm indeed produces a valid partition of the coin collection into  $i+1$  groups in which each one has a total sum no more than  $1.$  

Since we have exhausted all cases (when there exists a coin of denomination  $1$  and when there doesn't), we have concluded the inductive step. 

Hence, by the Principle of Mathematical Induction, we have proven the generalized version of the desired result, so we can just take  $k=100$  to conclude.  $\square$

Prove the more general statement: if there are a collection of finite coins with sum of values less than  $k - \frac{1}{2}$  then we can divide the collection into  $k$  groups with the sum of coin values in each group not exceeding 1.

Induct on  $k$ ; the base case is trivial. In the general case, if any subset of the finite coins has sum of values exactly  $1$ , we can put it into one group and induct immediately.

Otherwise, call coins with value  $1/m$  *big* if  $m \leq 2k$  and *small* otherwise.

First, for each big coin with value  $1/m$ , write  $m$  as the product of an odd number and power of two,  $m = 2^a \cdot \ell$ , and classify the big coins into  $k$  groups based on the value of  $\ell$  (there are  $k$  possible values of  $\ell$ , the odd numbers between  $1$  and  $2k - 1$ .) Now note that each group has sum less than  $1$ , because if any group's sum exceeded  $1$ , due to the way each coin is a power of two multiple of another, we could have found a subset with sum exactly  $1$  inside this group by greedily taking the largest coin, and then we'd have invoked the induction hypothesis.

So otherwise, we've put the big coins into groups. Now, we just take the small coins one by one and insert them into any group where they fit. If some coin  $1/m$  doesn't fit in any group, then every group sum is greater than  $1 - 1/m$ , so the total sum of values of coins already in the groups at that point is greater than  $k - k/m > k - 1/2$  since  $m$  is a small coin, a contradiction. Therefore this produces a valid division.

**General problem**

For  $r=1$  it is trivial. 

Now assume it is proven for  $r = 1,\cdots, R-1$ .
We will prove it now for  $r=R$ .

If there is a sum of some such reciprocals equal to  $1$ , we just take these in one group and by induction it will work for the other coins.

So, if it would be impossible, we can look to the coins with value equal to a fraction of  $S_1:$   $1, \frac{1}{2},  \frac{1}{2^2} \cdots$  $S_2:$  $\frac 13, \frac{1}{2*3},  \frac{1}{2^2*3} \cdots$  $\cdots $  $S_{R}:$   $\frac{1}{2R-1}, \frac{1}{2(2R-1)},\frac{1}{2^2(2R-1)}\cdots$  $\cdots$   (others)**CLAIM**
The sum of coins in  $S_i$  for  $1 \le i \le R$  is each time smaller than one.

This is possible, as  $min \{ S_i | i \le R\} \le \frac{R-0.5}{R} = 1 - \frac{1}{2R}$  and each new value is maximum  $\frac{1}{2R+1}$ .

We claim this uses up all coins in the pile. Assume not, and that some coin remains in the pile when all the boxes are saturated.

What was the motivation for combining coins with the same, even denominator?

The motivation is to "combine" **any** group of coins whose total value is itself an egyptian fraction, since that case **also** needs to be solvable. Thus, with even denominator  $2k$ , if we have two coins of  $\dfrac {1} {2k}$ , we should also be able to solve the case when we have instead one coin of  $\dfrac {1} {2k} + \dfrac {1} {2k} = \dfrac {1} {k}$ . With odd denominator  $2k+1$ , if we have  $2k+1$  coins of  $\dfrac {1} {2k+1}$ , we should also be able to solve the case when we have instead one coin of  $\dfrac {1} {2k+1} + \cdots + \dfrac {1} {2k+1} = 1$ . Several people in the above call this "optimization".

Then, place  $\frac{1}{2}$  into a seperate box of it's own, creating  $100$  boxes such that no two have total value more than  $1$ .

Given that we are reasonable human beings, we replace the number  $99$  with  $N$  and solve the problem for all non-negative  $N$ . Before solving the problem from here, we make a number of **Combinatorial Optimizations** which will help us solve the problem. In fact, these optimizations are forced upon us, since demanding them makes the problem strictly harder, yet the situation after making these optimizations is a case of the original problem.

    
- Remove all  $1$ s since they have to be in their own group.
- For all  $n$ , assume there is at most one  $\frac{1}{2n}$  coin, since two  $\frac{1}{2n}$  coins can be joined to make one  $\frac{1}{n}$  coin.
- For all odd  $n$ , assume there are at most  $n-1$   $\frac{1}{n}$  coins, since we can combine  $n$   $\frac{1}{n}$  coins into a  $1$  and delete them.

At this point, we can (almost) sit back and watch the problem solve itself. We create  $N+1$  groups labeled  $0,\ldots,N$ , and we place  $1/2$  in group  $0$ , and in box  $k$  we place all the  $\frac{1}{2k+1}$  coins and all the  $\frac{1}{2k+2}$  coins. This works as
\[\frac{2k}{2k+1}+\frac{1}{2k+2}\le 1.\]
At this point, we're left with coins of size at most  $\frac{1}{2N+3}$ . Place them into the current groups arbitrarily as long as we don't exceed  $1$ . If we ever get stuck, then each box has value at least  $1-\frac{1}{2N+3}$ , so the total value is at least
\[(N+1)\left(1-\frac{1}{2N+3}\right)=N+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4N+6}>N+\frac{1}{2},\]
a contradiction. This solves the problem.**Remark** Another (more extreme) example of this **Combinatorial Optimization** intuition is [USA TST 2017/1](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h1352165p12411381), where again, we make some forced optimizations, and this time *actually* sit back and watch the problem die.

Replace  $100$  and  $99\frac{1}{2}$  with  $n$  and  $n-\frac{1}{2}$  respectively. We will prove the claim with induction. The problem is trivial when  $n=1$ , so proceed to the inductive step. First, suppose that we have already put some coins into groups, and we are now unable to put in a coin of value  $v$ . Then, this means that all groups have value strictly greater than  $1-v$ , so  $n(1-v)+v< n-\frac{1}{2}\implies v> \frac{1}{2n-2}$ . So, if the denominator of any coin is  $2n-2$  or larger, we can ignore it, since it can always be put into a group.
Now, for coins with denominator between  $2$  and  $2n-2$ , note that if there are more than  $k-1$  coins of value  $\frac{1}{k}$ , then we can put  $k$  into one group to completely fill it up, and then use induction. So, assume that there are at most  $k-1$  such coins. Furthermore, if there are  $2$  coins of value  $\frac{1}{2k}$ , we can combine them into a single coin of value  $\frac{1}{k}$  and make the problem condition stricter. Thus, assume that there is at most one coin of any given even denominator. Given this, the total value of all coins with denominator of odd part  $p$  is at most   $$ \frac{p-1}{p}+\frac{1}{2p}+\frac{1}{4p}+\ldots = 1 $$   Thus, we can fit all such coins in a single group. As there are only  $n-1$  possible odd parts between  $2$  and  $2n-2$ , all coins can be put into  $n-1<n$  groups, as desired.

We'll solve a generalization for  $k, k-\frac{1}{2}$  instead of  $100, 99+\frac{1}{2}$ . First, put all coins of value  $1$  into their own group, and then combine every two coins of value  $\frac{1}{2m}$  into  $\frac{1}{m}$ , and finally, whenever there are at least  $x$  coins of value  $\frac{1}{x}$ , keep making groups of  $1$  out of them until we can't anymore. Hence, we can WLOG let there be at most  $2m-2$  coins of  $\frac{1}{2m-1}$  and at most one coin of  $\frac{1}{2m}$ , for each  $m$ .

Now, make  $k$  groups, and for each  $m\in [1, k]$ , put all the coins of  $\frac{1}{2m}$  and  $\frac{1}{2m-1}$  in group  $m$ . This won't overfill any groups because  $\frac{1}{2m}+\frac{2m-2}{2m-1}<1$ . After this, the only coins left are  $\frac{1}{2k+1}$  and smaller. But note that since the groups right now sum to at most  $k-\frac{1}{2}$ , the total waste is at least  $\frac{1}{2}$ , meaning there is a group with waste at least  $\frac{1}{2k}$  and we can take a leftover coin and put it in that group. But the total waste will never go below  $\frac{1}{2}$ , so we can keep repeating what we just did until all the coins are placed in a group, and hence we are done.

First, we can remove all  $1$ s. Then, we can combine every pair of coins with the value  $\frac{1}{2i}$  to make coins of value  $\frac{1}{i}$ . Finally, for every group of  $2i+1$  coins of value  $\frac{1}{2i+1}$ , we can group them to make a  $1$ . Then, we can remove all of these groups and induct downwards, so that we have to prove the result for  $k$  groups with total value at most  $k-\frac12$ . 

Now, at this point, there is at most  $1$  coin with the value  $\frac{1}{2i}$  and at most  $2i$  coins with the value  $\frac{1}{2i+1}$ . In the first group, we can place the coin with value  $\frac{1}{2}$  if it exists. In the group  $1<i \le k$ , we can place all the coins with values  $\frac{1}{2i-1}$  and  $\frac{1}{2i}$ .  It is easy to see that the total value in each of these groups is less than  $1$  because the total value is at most
\[ (2i-2) \cdot \frac{1}{2i-1} + \frac{1}{2i} < 1. \]
Then, we can place all of the remaining coins into any of these groups as long as the value in each group is less than  $1$ . We can do this because the value of each remaining coin is at most  $\frac{1}{2k+1}$ . It would only be impossible if the total value was at least
\[ k \left( 1 -\frac{1}{2k+1} \right) > k - \frac12, \]
which is a contradiction.

Say there are  $m+1/2$  coins and  $m+1$  groups desired. For any collection of  $n$  coins each with value  $1/n$ , merge them into one group to reduce the problem to the case of at most  $m-1/2$  total sum and  $m$  groups desired. Then, merge any two coins with value  $1/n,1/k$  such that  $\frac{1}{n}+\frac{1}{k}=\frac{1}{\ell}$  for some integer  $\ell$ . After iterating this, merge any collection of three coins with sum in 
\[S=\left\{\frac{1}{n}\mid n\in \mathbb{N}\right\},\]
and so on. At any point when there are  $n$  coins each with value  $1/n$ , merge them into one group. After all this iteration, there are at most  $n-1$  coins with any value  $1/n$  and any set of coins with size at least  $2$  have sum that is not a valid coinage. 

Now, we demonstrate an algorithm that enables us to win. List the coins in monotonically decreasing order of value, so if the coin values for  $x_1,\dots , x_\ell$  we have  $x_1\ge x_2\ge \cdots \ge x_\ell$ . At the  $i$ -th stage, we add coin  $i$ . Let the groups at this stage be  $1,\dots , a$  for some integer  $a$ . Let group  $j$  have  $y_j$  total value. Add coin  $i$  to the group  $j$  such that  $y_j+x_i \le 1$  (actually  $y_j+x_i<1$  by our manipulations earlier) and  $j$  is minimal. If there exists no such group  $j$ , append group  $a+1$  including just coin  $i$ . 

We show that this algorithm preserves the condition  $\sum_{j=1}^i x_j \le m+1/2\implies a\le m$ . Note that it suffices to show that appending group  $a+1$  implies  $\sum_{j=1}^ix_j>a+1/2$ . Now, remark that
\[\sum_{j=1}^ix_j = \sum_{j=1}^a y_j+x_i.\]
By the definition of our algorithm, appending group  $a+1$  implies  $y_j>1-x_i$  for all  $j$ , hence
\[\sum_{j=1}^ix_j = \sum_{j=1}^a y_j+x_i > a(1-x_i)+x_i = a-(a-1)x_i.\]
Thus, it suffices to demonstrate
\[(a-1)x_i \le \frac{1}{2}.\]
Now, recall that by our earlier simplifications, we can assume that for any odd positive integer  $n$ , there are at most  $n-1$  instances of  $x_j$  equal to  $1/n$  and for any even positive integer  $n$  there is at most one instance of  $x_j$  equal to  $1/n$ . Let  $x_i = 1/b$ . We have the bound
\[a< \frac{3}{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} x_j\]
by the inductive hypothesis applied to  $i-1$ . At this point, we also remark that the base case trivially holds; there is just one group. Now, we take cases: either  $b$  is even or it is odd. Let  $b=2c-1$  or  $b=2c$ .**Case 1**: We have  $b=2c$ . Observe that
\[a-1< \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3-1}{3}+\cdots + \frac{2c-2}{2c-1}+\frac{1}{2c} < 1+\frac{3-1}{3}+\frac{1}{4}+\cdots + \frac{2c-2}{2c-1}+\frac{1}{2c} = c,\]
which rearranges to imply the desired.**Case 2**: We have  $b=2c-1$ . Observe that
\[a-1< \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3-1}{3}+\cdots + \frac{2c-2}{2c-1} < c - \frac{1}{2c-1},\]
hence  $a-1\le c-1$ , which rearranges to imply the desired.

stem_md:
A set of lines in the plane is in *general position* if no two are parallel and no three pass through the same point. A set of lines in general position cuts the plane into regions, some of which have finite area; we call these its *finite regions*. Prove that for all sufficiently large  $n$ , in any set of  $n$  lines in general position it is possible to colour at least  $\sqrt{n}$  lines blue in such a way that none of its finite regions has a completely blue boundary.

*Note*: Results with  $\sqrt{n}$  replaced by  $c\sqrt{n}$  will be awarded points depending on the value of the constant  $c$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Preface</summary>Here's my proof for  $c=1$  ( $n$  is arbitrary). I have compared it with other proofs already posted and have found that the closest is oneplusone's. However, there are some differences.

First, I didn't need to color **points**, only **lines** was to be colored.
Second (as the consequence of first), the proof of workability of the algorithm was made in terms of borders of suspicious polygon and not in terms of his vertices.

Also note that some lines may be parallel, so corresponding stipulation is redundant in the statement of the problem (it is not redundant in the conventional definition of a *general position* though).</details>

Let  $\mathcal A(k,l,m)$  denote that the lines  $l$  and  $m$  intersect the line  $k$  at adjacent points (i.e. they are not parallel to  $k$  and there is no line  $u$  such that  $k \cap u$  lies between  $k \cap l$  and  $k \cap m$  on  $k$ ). Since all points at which any line  $k$  is intersected by other lines can be ordered according to some direction on  $k$ , for each pair of distinct lines  $(k,l)$  there can be no more than two lines  $m$  such that  $\mathcal A(k,l,m)$ .

Now to the coloring algorithm. Initially, all lines are grey and  $i=1$ .

<u>Step i</u>  Take any grey line, color it blue and denote by  $b_i$ . For each  $j<i$  (when  $i>1$ ), take any grey line  $g$  such that  $\mathcal A(b_j,b_i,g)$  and color it red.
Increase  $i$  and repeat the step until there are no grey lines left.

*Proof that the algorithm returns at least  $\sqrt n$  blue lines.*
Note that after  $i$  steps, there are exactly  $i$  blue lines and at most  $i(i-1)$  red ones. Indeed, at the  $i^{\text{\tiny th}}$  step at most  $2(i-1)$  red lines were added (recall the above note on the number of  $g$  such that  $\mathcal A(b_j,b_i,g)$  for a given pair  $(b_j,b_i)$ , where  $j=1,\dots,i-1$ ), and the total number of red lines after  $i$  steps is at most  $2(1+2+\dots+(i-1))=i(i-1)$ . Thus, at least  $n-(i+i(i-1))=n-i^2$  grey lines remain after  $i$  steps. So when the current number of blue lines  $i$  is less than  $\sqrt n$ , we can continue the process.

*Proof that none of finite regions has a completely blue boundary after the end of the algorithm.*
Suppose such a region exists. As it is finite, it is bounded by at least 3 blue lines. Let  $b_j$  be the line having minimum index among them, and  $b_p$  along with  $b_q$  be two lines forming adjacent sides of the region. WLOG  $p<q$ . Since  $j<p$  and  $\mathcal A(b_j,b_p,b_q)$ , the line  $b_q$  had to be colored red at the  $p^{\text{\tiny th}}$  step. Contradiction.  $\blacksquare$

We construct a planar graph with vertices the intersection points of the lines and an edge between two vertices if and only if the vertices are consecutive intersection points in one of those lines.

We have  $V = \binom{n}{2}$  vertices and  $E = n(n-2)$  edges and so we have  $F = 1 + E - V = \cdots = \binom{n-1}{2} \leqslant n^2/2$  bounded faces.

We colour some of the lines blue independently at random with probability  $p$ . We call a face bad if all its edges are colour blue. Let X be the number of coloured lines minus the number of bad faces. Then  $EX \geqslant np - p^3n^2/2$ . Choosing \[ p = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3n}}\] we obtain  $EX \geqslant (2/3)^{3/2} \sqrt{n}$ . 

So there is a colouring of the lines such that the number of coloured lines minus the number of bad faces is at least  $(2/3)^{3/2} \sqrt{n}$ . We decolour at list one line from each bad face. We now have no bad faces and at least  $(2/3)^{3/2} \sqrt{n}$  coloured lines.

We call 2 points (on a line) neighbors if there are no other points on the line segment joining those 2. Then each finite region has to be a convex polygon whose any pair of neighboring vertices are, well, neighbors. Now start by coloring any line blue, and all points are uncolored (neither red nor blue).

Suppose there is an uncolored line which does not pass through any red points. Color that line blue. Now consider each of the intersections that line makes with the other blue lines. For each intersection point  $X$  of the 2 blue lines  $l_1,l_2$ , color it blue (it was originally uncolored). Now consider the neighbors of  $X$  on  $l_1,l_2$ , call them  $A_1,A_2$  on  $l_1$  and  $B_1,B_2$  on  $l_2$  (if there is only 1 neighbor, let the other point be an uncolored dummy). If neither  $A_1$  nor  $A_2$  is blue, we colour them both red. Else if neither  $B_1$  nor  $B_2$  is blue, we colour them both red. Otherwise, we colour the uncolored ones (out of the 4 points) red. Anyway, we would have colored at most 2 points red. Once we have done this for all the intersection points, proceed back to the start of this paragraph until no such line exists.

Now to show it works. Suppose there is a finite region polygon  $P_1...P_m$  with all blue boundaries (with  $P_{m+1}=P_1$ ). Then all the points must be blue. Consider the first point colored blue, WLOG let it be  $P_2$ . Suppose the previous line to be colored blue is  $P_1P_2$ . Then  $P_2P_3$  has to be colored blue before that, and  $P_3P_4$  has to be uncolored (otherwise  $P_3$  will be colored blue first). So  $P_3$  is uncolored. Then if  $P_1$  is blue,  $P_3$  will be colored red by our coloring algorithm.  $P_1$  has to be uncolored and by our coloring algorithm at least one of  $P_1,P_3$  will be colored red. Note that no blue line will pass through a red point. Thus there are no finite region with blue boundaries.

Now suppose  $k$  lines are blue. By our algorithm, each blue point intersection will introduce at most 2 red points. Since we can't color any more lines blue, those red points will cover the remaining lines. Thus  $2\binom{k}{2}\geq n-k\implies k\geq \sqrt{n}$  exact.

The main core of the proof is the following lemma.**Lovasz Local Lemma** Consider several events, each occurring with probability at most  $p$ , such that each event is independent fexcept for at most  $d$  of them. If \[ epd \le 1 \] then there is a nonzero probability that no events happen.

Split the  $n$  lines into  $c \sqrt n$  groups of size  $\frac{\sqrt n}{c}$  each, arbitrarily.  We are going to select one line from each of the groups at random to be blue.  For each of the regions  $R_1$ ,  $R_2$ , \dots,  $R_m$  we will consider an event  $A_k$  meaning ``three of the lines bounding  $R_k$  are blue''; we designate these lines beforehand.  We will show there is a nonzero probability that no events occur.

The probability of  $A_k$  is clearly at most  $\left( \frac{c}{\sqrt n} \right)^3$ .

For each  $R_k$ , we have three groups to consider. Each group consists of  $\sqrt n$  lines. Each line is part of at most  $2n-2$  regions.
Hence  $A_k$  depends on at most  $3 \cdot \sqrt n \cdot (2n-2)$  events.

Thus,
\[ e \left( \frac{c}{\sqrt n} \right)^3 \left( 3 \cdot \sqrt{n} \cdot (2n-2) \right)
	< 6ec^3 = 1 \]
and we are done by LLL.
