stem_md: Let  $P_n(x)=1+2x+3x^2+\cdots+nx^{n-1}.$  Prove that the polynomials  $P_j(x)$  and  $P_k(x)$  are relatively prime for all positive integers  $j$  and  $k$  with  $j\ne k.$
solution_md:
<details><summary>References/introductory comments</summary>This is definitely not the intended solution (and no, I didn't get it during the test---I spent a long time on it afterwards). But I'm glad I found it---I think it ties together lots of nice ideas from number theory.

Nothing here is actually very deep; everything used below can probably be found [here](http://math.mit.edu/~ebelmont/785-notes.pdf) (Eva Belmont's notes for MIT 18.785 Fall 2014) or [here](https://www.sharelatex.com/project/54079c9cebf2980f305c6ef2) (my notes). Some specific references for the  $p$ -adic methods below: Koblitz, PFTB/SFTB, and a (Wordpress) blog post I hope to write soon (based on a bad MIT SCUM talk I gave titled ``18.100 $p$ '').

Please let me know if anything is unclear.</details>

===

<details><summary>Standard setup</summary>After checking that  $0$  isn't a common root, rephrase the problem in terms of the (monic) reciprocal polynomials  $Q_n(x) := \frac{x^n+\cdots+x - n}{x-1}$ . Check, by triangle inequality, that  $|\alpha| > 1$  for any common root (as one of  $k,j \ne 1$ ). So  $|f(0)| \mid \gcd(k,j)$  gives  $\gcd(k,j) > 1$ .

Let  $\alpha$  be a common root of  $Q_k,Q_j$ , and  $f\in \mathbb{Q}[x]$  its (monic) minimal polynomial over  $\mathbb{Q}$ . Then the roots of  $f$  are all algebraic integers, so  $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$  (this works in more general settings too where Gauss' lemma argument fails).</details>

<details><summary>Basic NT setup</summary>Take  $p\mid k,j$  (whether or not  $p\mid f(0)$ ) and take an embedding of [the splitting field of  $f$ ] into  $\mathbb{C}_p$  (this is not unique if there's more than one prime ideal  $\wp\mid p$  over  $p$ ). If  $v_p(\alpha) > 0$ , then  $-k = \alpha^{k+1} - (k+1)\alpha$  yields  $v_p(\alpha) = v_p(k) > 0$ . But  $f(0)/\alpha$  is an algebraic integer, so  $v_p(f(0)) \ge v_p(\alpha) > 0$  means  $p\mid f(0)$ . Then  $v_p(\alpha') \le v_p(f(0)) - v_p(\alpha) \le v_p(k) - v_p(\alpha) = 0$  for the conjugates  $\alpha'$  of  $\alpha$ .

But  $\deg{f} > 1$  trivially, so we may WLOG assume  $v_p(\alpha) = 0$ . So  $v_p(n) = v_p(\frac{\alpha^n - 1}{\alpha - 1})$  for  $n = k,j$ . Then using lifting argument below easy to show  $v_p(\alpha^{\gcd(k,j)} - 1) = v_p(\gcd(k,j)(\alpha-1)) \ge 1$ .

For details near the end, it will help to think about equality cases---the inequality is strict *unless*  $v_p(\gcd(k,j)) = 1$  and  $v_p(\alpha-1) = 0$ . But  $\text{ord}_\wp(\alpha) \mid p^{f_\wp} - 1$  (here  $\wp\subset \overline{\mathbb{Q}_p} \subset \mathbb{C}_p$  is a prime of  $\mathbb{Q}_p(\alpha)$  lying over  $p\mathbb{Z}_p$ ), so  $\gcd(k,j)$  shares a prime factor with  $p^{f_\wp} - 1$ . **Thus if equality holds, then  $\gcd(k,j)$  is not a power of  $p$ , and we could've originally chosen a different  $p'\mid \gcd(k,j)$ .** (We'll use this for  $p=3$  later on.)</details>

<details><summary>Somewhat aside: lifting the exponent in number fields</summary>Let  $p\in \mathbb{Z}$  and  $\wp\mid p$  a prime (in a ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$ ) over  $\mathbb{Z}$ .

Look at  $\alpha\in \mathcal{O}_K$ , with  $\wp\nmid \alpha$ . We want to study  $v_\wp(\alpha^n - 1)$  for  $n\ge1$ . From  $[\mathcal{O}_K / \wp \mathcal{O}_K : \mathbb{F}_p] = f_\wp$  we have  $\ell := \text{ord}_\wp(\alpha) \mid p^{f_\wp} - 1$ . So  $p\nmid \ell$ . The interesting case is when  $\ell \mid n$  (i.e.  $\alpha^n \equiv 1\pmod\wp$ ); here
\[ v_\wp(\frac{\alpha^n - 1}{\alpha^\ell - 1}) = \sum_{t=0}^{v_p(n)-1} v_\wp(\frac{\alpha^{p^{t+1}\ell} - 1}{\alpha^{p^t\ell} - 1}), \] where we've used the fact that  $\frac{\alpha^n - 1}{\alpha^{p^{v_p(n)}\ell} - 1} \equiv \frac{n}{p^{v_p(n)}\ell} \not\equiv 0 \pmod{\wp}$ .

Mimicking usual LTE, when  $\wp\mid u-1$ , look at \[ \frac{u^p - 1}{u - 1} = \sum_{t=1}^{p} \binom{p}{t} (u-1)^{t-1} = p + (u-1)^{p-1} + \sum_{t=2}^{p-1} \binom{p}{t} (u-1)^{t-1}, \] where for  $2\le t\le p-1$  the  $\binom{p}{t} (u-1)^{t-1}$  terms are divisible by  $p\wp \equiv 0\pmod{\wp^{e_\wp + 1}}$ . So the important terms are  $p$  and  $(u-1)^{p-1}$ , with  $v_\wp(p) = e_\wp$  and  $v_\wp((u-1)^{p-1}) = (p-1) v_\wp(u-1)$ .

In particular, if  $v_\wp(u-1) > \frac{e_\wp}{p-1}$ , then  $v_\wp(\frac{u^p - 1}{u-1}) = e_\wp$ . [This is **not** analogous to the degeneracy of  $p=2$  in usual LTE.]</details>

<details><summary>Finish 1: Skolem-Mahler-Lech exponentials/linear recurrence approach</summary>Indeed, what follows is essentially a special case of (the method behind) the [Skolem-Mahler-Lech theorem](http://terrytao.wordpress.com/2007/05/25/open-question-effective-skolem-mahler-lech-theorem/); I originally saw this several years ago in PFTB, and more recently revisited it via SFTB. (See similar concrete manifestations [here](http://math.stackexchange.com/questions/705877/an-exotic-sequence) and [here](http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Forum/viewtopic.php?f=57&t=598357).) I hope to clarify the intuition and unity behind these approaches in my aforementioned upcoming blog post.

Let  $\beta := \alpha^{(k,j)} - 1$ . Then for  $m = k/(k,j), j/(k,j)$  we have
\[ 1 + m(k,j)(1-\alpha^{-1}) = \alpha^{m(k,j)} = (1+\beta)^m = 1 + m\beta + \binom{m}{2} \beta^2 + \cdots \] (for context,  $m\mapsto (1+\beta)^m$  is a continuous, in fact analytic,  $p$ -adic function from  $\mathbb{Z}_p\to \mathbb{C}_p$ ; this is the easy direction of Mahler's theorem on said continuous functions), so
\begin{align*}
\frac{(k,j)(1-\alpha^{-1})-\beta}{\beta^2}
&= \binom{m-1}{1}\frac12 + \binom{m-1}{2}\frac{\beta}{3} + \binom{m-1}{3}\frac{\beta^2}{4} + \cdots 
&= (m-1)\frac{1}{2} + (m-1)(m-2)\frac{\beta}{3!} + (m-1)(m-2)(m-3)\frac{\beta^2}{4!} + \cdots.
\end{align*} The intuition is that ``locally, this looks linear in  $m$ '' (and indeed, we could rewrite this as a power series in  $m$  if we wanted). But anyway, let  $k' = k/(k,j)$  and  $j' = j/(k,j)$ ; then plugging in  $m=k',j'$  and subtracting (and dividing by  $k'-j'\ne0$ ) gives
\[ 0 = c_0 + c_1 \beta + c_2\beta^2 + \cdots \in \frac12 + \frac{\mathbb{Z}}{\operatorname{lcm}(1,2,3)} \beta + \frac{\mathbb{Z}}{\operatorname{lcm}(1,2,3,4)} \beta^2 + \cdots, \] where  $c_i = \frac{1}{i+2} \frac{\binom{k'-1}{i+1} - \binom{j'-1}{i+1}}{k'-j'}$  and we're noting by Vandermonde's identity that
\begin{align*}
\frac{\binom{k'-1}{N} - \binom{k'-j'}{0}\binom{j'-1}{N}}{k'-j'}
&= \sum_{z=1}^{N} \frac{1}{k'-j'}\binom{k'-j'}{z} \binom{j'-1}{N-z} 
&= \sum_{z=1}^{N} \frac{1}{z}\binom{k'-j'-1}{z-1} \binom{j'-1}{N-z} 
\in \frac{\mathbb{Z}}{\operatorname{lcm}(1,2,\ldots,N)}.
\end{align*} (Cf. [USA TST 2009 Problem 3](http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Forum/viewtopic.php?f=57&t=289583&).)

[Note that without Vandermonde, one can easily get  $c_i \in \frac{\mathbb{Z}}{(i+2)!}$  (and the less useful  $c_i \in \frac{\mathbb{Z}}{(i+2)(k'-j')}$ ). We'll only need the stronger lcm estimate for  $p=2,3$ . Indeed, the following crude bound on the lcm (i.e. comparing with the corresponding factorial) will suffice in most cases:
\begin{align*}
v_p(c_t \beta^t)
&\ge v_p(\beta^t / \operatorname{lcm}(1,2,\ldots,t+2)) 
&\ge v_p(\beta^t / (t+2)!) \ge t - \frac{t+2-s_p(t+2)}{p-1} \ge t-\frac{t+1}{p-1},
\end{align*}
where for  $p=2,3$  it may help to note that the inequality is strict if  $v_p(\beta) > 1$ .]

If  $p \ge 5$ , the  $\beta^t/(t+2)!$  terms are all divisible by  $p$  (i.e.  $v_p(\cdot) \ge 1$ ), so we get  $0 \equiv \frac12 \pmod{p}$ , which is absurd.

If  $p=2$ , we use the stronger Vandermonde bound. Since  $v_2(\beta^t/\operatorname{lcm}(1,2,\ldots,t+2)) \ge 0$  for all  $t \ge 1$  (the worst case is  $t = 2^s - 2$  for  $s\ge 2$ , but  $2^s - 2 \ge s$  here), taking modulo  $1$  gives  $0 \equiv \frac12 \pmod{2^0}$ , contradiction. So we're good to go if  $p=2$ .

If  $p=3$  and  $v_3(\beta) > 1$ , then looking mod  $3$  gives  $0 \equiv \frac12 \pmod3$ , which is absurd. **On the other hand, if  $v_3(\beta) = 1$ ,** then recall from above that some prime  $q \ne 3$  divides  $\gcd(k,j)$ , so our arguments for  $p\ne 3$  (above) will work.</details>

\begin{align*}
\frac{n}{(k,j)} \log_p(\alpha^{(k,j)})
= \log_p(\alpha^n)
&= \log_p(1 + n(1-\alpha^{-1})) 
& = \sum_{i\ge1} (-1)^{i+1}\frac{[n(1-\alpha^{-1})]^i}{i}.
\end{align*} Thus
\[ \frac{1}{(k,j)} \log_p(\alpha^{(k,j)}) = \sum_{i\ge1} (-1)^{i+1}\frac{(1-\alpha^{-1})^i}{i} n^{i-1}. \] Now plugging in  $n = k,j$  and subtracting gives
\begin{align*}
0
&= \sum_{i\ge1} (-1)^{i+1}\frac{(1-\alpha^{-1})^i}{i} [k^{i-1} - j^{i-1}] 
&= (k-j)\sum_{z\ge1} (-1)^{z+2}\frac{(1-\alpha^{-1})^{z+1}}{z+1} \frac{k^z - j^z}{k-j}.
\end{align*}

If  $p \ge 5$  this easily gives a contradiction modulo  $p(1-\alpha^{-1})^2$ . I believe that  $p=2$  and  $p=3$  can be fleshed out similarly as in the Skolem-Mahler-Lech approach.</details>

<details><summary>Sketch of Bobby's solution (I believe fleshed out after the test by David Yang, Mitchell Lee, and possibly Mark Sellke)</summary>Suppose for sake of contradiction that  $Q_k(\alpha) = Q_j(\alpha) = 0$  for some complex  $\alpha \ne 0,1$ . Then for  $n=k,j$  we have  $\alpha^{n+1} = (n+1)\alpha - n = \alpha + (\alpha-1)n$ , so
\[ A(n) := |\alpha|^{2n+2} = |\alpha + (\alpha-1)n|^2 = |\alpha|^2 + 2\Re(\alpha^2-\alpha) n + |\alpha-1|^2 n^2 =: B(n). \] Here  $A:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}_{>0}$  is a positive exponential function over the reals, and  $B:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}$  is a polynomial over the reals of degree at most  $2$ .

We have  $A(k) = B(k)$  and  $A(j) = B(j)$  by assumption. But there are also (a priori) ``degenerate solutions''  $A(0) = B(0)$  and  $A(-1) = B(-1)$ . Yet by a standard Rolle's theorem argument, a (nonzero) exponential and a quadratic can intersect at no more than  $3$  points, contradiction.</details>**Remark.** It seems to be open whether the  $P_n(x)$  (or equivalently  $Q_n(x)$ ) are irreducible over  $\mathbb{Q}$ . Prasolov's excellent *Polynomials* book. The details certainly seem delicate, but it's intuitively pretty plausible.

Algebraically, the most ambitious approach would be to try proving irreducibility (currently open according to above Remark) or at least get a lot of information on irreducible factors. Of course, it would be amusing if the http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resultant were tractable (e.g. via http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvester_matrix ). But this feels extremely unlikely.</details>

No, it does not. $f(x)=x$ and $g(x)=x^2-x$ are linearly independent. That is, if $a$ and $b$ are scalars (constants), and $af(x)+bg(x)$ is the zero polynomial, then $a=b=0.$ But $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are not relatively prime, since their g.c.d. as polynomials is $x,$ which is not constant. More dramatically: $\{1,x,x^2,x^3,\dots\}$ is an infinite independent set in the vector space of all polynomials, In fact, this set is a basis for that vector space. But in the *algebra* of polynomials, every non-constant element of this set is a multiple of $x.$ Hence the elements of this set are very far from being relatively prime. A vector space has two operations: addition and multiplication by scalars. A ring has a different set of two operations: addition and multiplication of elements. An algebra is both a vector space and a ring, so there are three operations: addition, multiplication by scalars, and multiplication of elements. The words "relatively prime" make sense in a ring (hence an algebra). They do not make sense in a set that is only considered to be a vector space.

\]

\[

(note that  $|w|$  and  $\mathrm{Re}(w)$  are real constants), it has at least  $4$  distinct roots. stem_md: Let  $n$  be a positive integer. What is the largest  $k$  for which there exist  $n\times n$  matrices  $M_1,\dots,M_k$  and  $N_1,\dots,N_k$  with real entries such that for all  $i$  and  $j,$  the matrix product  $M_iN_j$  has a zero entry somewhere on its diagonal if and only if  $i\ne j?$
solution_md:
I just saw a comment about tensor product on the problem by pythag011 and trying to elaborate on the same...

Firstly, we get rid of the trash in the configuration, which are the matrices. Once we formulate the problem in the proper set up the answer will come out very easily.

So there are precisely  $k$  elements  $M_1, \ldots, M_k$  in  $\prod_{i=1}^{n}{R} ^{n}$  for which there exists another set of  $k$  elements  $L_1, \ldots, L_k$  in  $ \prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{R}^{n}$  such that  $\phi (M_i,L_j) =0$  iff  $i \ne j$ , where  $\phi$  is function from   $\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{R}^{n} \times \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{R}^{n} \to \mathbb{R}$ , defined as  $\phi \left ((u_1, \ldots, u_n), ( v_1, \ldots, v_n) \right) = \prod_{i} ( u_i \cdot v_i) \in \mathbb R$ . That's all the matrices,multiplication and diagonal entries have to say. 

(Where  $u_i, v_j$ -s are vectors in  $ \mathbb{R}^n$ , and the dot denotes the scalar product.)

Now it's easily seen that  $\phi$  is linear in each of the  $u_i, v_j$ -s. Hence  $\phi$ , being a multi-linear map, defines a well-defined map in the tensor product (by the universal property) which we will also denote by  $\phi$ . So we restate the conditions again as follows:
Consider  $T= \bigotimes_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{R}^n$ .Our  $\phi $  is a  $\mathbb R$ -module map from  $T \otimes T$  to  $\mathbb{R}$ . The problem now becomes: Let  $M_1, \ldots, M_k$  be elementary tensors in  $T$  for which there are elementary tensors  $L_1, \ldots, L_k$  in  $T$  such that  $\phi(M_i \otimes L_j) = 0$  iff  $i \ne j$ .



Now the  $M_i$ -s form a linearly independent set, as can be seen by taking any linear relation and applying  $\phi ( \,\cdot \otimes L_j)$  for all  $1 \le j \le k$ . Since  $\dim T = n^n$  (tensor product of free modules is free), we must have  $k \le n^n$ .

stem_md: A *base* 10 *over-expansion* of a positive integer  $N$  is an expression of the form  $N=d_k10^k+d_{k-1}10^{k-1}+\cdots+d_0 10^0$  with  $d_k\ne 0$  and  $d_i\in\{0,1,2,\dots,10\}$  for all  $i.$  For instance, the integer  $N=10$  has two base 10 over-expansions:  $10=10\cdot 10^0$  and the usual base 10 expansion  $10=1\cdot 10^1+0\cdot 10^0.$  Which positive integers have a unique base 10 over-expansion?
solution_md:
In easy language.

He claim that the number having non-zero digits is the required positive integers having unique base 10 over-expansion.

Suppose an arbitrary number  $N=\overline{a_na_{n-1}....a_1a_0}$ , where  $a_i\neq 0$  for  $i\in [n]$ . $N=a_n\cdot 10^n +...+ a_k\cdot 10^k +a_{k-1}\cdot 10^{k-1}+.......=a_n\cdot 10^n+...+(a_k-1)\cdot 10^k +(a_{k-1}+10)\cdot 10^{k-1}+.......$ .
But  $a_{k-1}+10>10$  which is a contradiction!
Hence proved.

$N$  has a unique over-expansion if and only if its ordinary decimal expansion has no zeros.

First, suppose that the decimal expansion of  $N$  has no zeros. That is,  $N=\sum_{k=0}^m d_k10^k$  where  $d_k\in\{1,2,\dots,9\}.$  Suppose also  $N=\sum_{k=0}^{m'}e_k10^k$  where  $e_k$  is also allowed to be  $0$  or  $10.$   Note that  $N\equiv d_0\pmod{10}$  and  $N\equiv e_0\pmod{10},$  so  $d_0\equiv e_k\pmod{10}.$  But with  $1\le d_0\le 9,$  the only way to satisfy this congruence is to have  $e_0=d_0.$ Now, suppose we have proved that  $e_k=d_k$  for  $0\le k\le j.$  Consider the number  $10^{-j}\left(N-\sum_{k=0}^jd_k10^k\right),$  and find what it is congruent to  $\mod{10}.$  By a very similar argument to the above, we find that  $e_{j+1}=d_{j+1}.$  So by induction, we conclude that  $e_k=d_k$  for all  $k$  and the over-expansion is unique.

For the converse, suppose that  $N$  has a decimal expansion that has at least one zero. Let  $d_j$  be the left-most such zero, which implies that  $d_j=0$  and  $d_{j+1}\ne 0.$  Hence a two-digit portion of the expansion is  $d_{j+1}10^{j+1}+0.$  Note that this equals  $(d_{j+1}-1)10^{j+1}+10\cdot 10^j.$  So we let  $e_j=10$  and  $e_{j+1}=d_{j+1}-1$  to get a different over-expansion. (Note: if it happens that  $d_{j+1}=1$  and that was the left-most digit, then we omit that digit from the new over-expansion, which now has one fewer digit.)

This is not part of the solution, but in order to actually write down over-expansions, I used the symbol X as the symbol for 10 as a digit. Hence we can write 103 as X3, or 203 as 1X3, or 2030 as 1X30 or 202X or 1X2X. We can write 110 as 10X or XX.

I prove that ***$N$  does not have a unique base-10 expansion if and only if  $N$  has a digit  $0$  in its standard base-10 expression. (*)*****$( \Rightarrow)$  If  $N$  does not have a unique base-10 expansion:**
Then in the expression \[N = \sum_{i=0}^k d_i \cdot 10^i \ (0 \le d_i \le 10 \ \forall i, d_k \ne 0)\] there exists  $i$  such that  $d_i = 10$ .
Let  $S = \{ i \ | \ d_i = 10 \}$  and let  $m = \min S \Rightarrow d_m = 10 ; d_i < 10 \ \forall i < m$ .
We can write  $N$  as \[\begin{aligned} N & = d_k \cdot 10^k + d_{k-1} \cdot 10^{k-1} + \ldots + d_{m+1} \cdot 10^{m+1} + 10 \cdot 10^m + d_{m-1} \cdot 10^{m-1} + \ldots + d_1 \cdot 10 + d_0  & = d_k \cdot 10^k + d_{k-1} \cdot 10^{k-1} + \ldots  + (d_{m+1} + 1) \cdot 10^{m+1} + 0 \cdot 10^m + d_{m-1} \cdot 10^{m-1} + \ldots + d_1 \cdot 10 + d_0. \end{aligned}\]
We know that the coefficient of  $10^m$  is  $0$ , otherwise it must be the case that  $d_{m-1} = 10$ , but this contradicts our definition of  $m$ .
In other words,  $N$ 's standard base-10 expression is \[\overline{a_n a_{n-1} a_{n-2} \ldots a_{m+1} 0\ d_{m-1} \ldots d_1 d_0}\] and it contains at least one digit  $0$ . (QED)
(we know that  $d_0, d_1, \ldots, d_{m-1}$  are already within  $[0;9]$  so they are also the digits of the standard base-10. But we don't know about  $d_{m+1}, d_{m+2}, \ldots, d_k$  so we have to introduce new variables  $n$  and  $a_{m+1}, a_{m+2}, \ldots, a_n$  instead)**$(\Leftarrow)$  If  $N$  has a digit  $0$  in its standard base-10 expression:**
Consider the standard base-10 expression of  $N$ : \[N = \sum_{i=0}^n a_i \cdot 10^i \ (0 \le a_i \le 9 \ \forall i, a_n \ne 0)\]
Let  $S = \{ i \ | \ a_i = 0 \}$  and let  $m = \max S \Rightarrow a_{m} = 0 ; a_i > 0 \ \forall i > m$ .
We can write  $N$  as \[\begin{aligned} N &= a_n \cdot 10^n + a_{n-1} \cdot 10^{n-1} + \ldots + a_{m+1} \cdot 10^{m+1} + 0 \cdot a_m + a_{m-1} \cdot 10^{m-1} + \ldots + a_1 \cdot 10 + a_0  & = a_n \cdot 10^n + a_{n-1} \cdot 10^{n-1} + \ldots + (a_{m+1}-1) \cdot 10^{m+1} + 10 \cdot 10^m + a_{m-1} \cdot 10^{m-1} + \ldots + a_1 \cdot 10 + a_0 \end{aligned}\]
So  $N$  does not have a unique base-10 expansion.
Thus we have proven (*), from which we can infer that ***$N$  has a unique base-10 expansion if and only if  $N$  does not have a digit  $0$  in its standard base-10 expression.***

stem_md: Suppose that  $f$  is a function on the interval  $[1,3]$  such that  $-1\le f(x)\le 1$  for all  $x$  and  $\displaystyle \int_1^3f(x)\,dx=0.$  How large can  $\displaystyle\int_1^3\frac{f(x)}x\,dx$  be?
solution_md:
Suppose that $f$ is an integrable function on the interval $[1,3]$ such that $-1\le f(x)\le 1$ for all $x$ and $\displaystyle \int_1^3f(x)\,dx=0.$ How large can $\displaystyle\int_1^3\frac{f(x)}x\,dx$ be?
The answer is $\boxed{\ln \left( \frac{4}{3} \right)}$ , where equality holds if and only if $f(x)= g(x)$ , where we define \begin{align*} g(x) = \begin{cases} -1 \ &\text{if } 1 \le x < 2 1 \ &\text{if } 2 < x \le 3 c \ &\text{if } x = 2 \end{cases} \end{align*} where $c \in [-1,1]$ be any constant. Indeed, We could check that \begin{align*} \int_1^3 \frac{g(x)}{x} dx &= \int_1^2 \frac{g(x)}{x} dx + \int_2^3 \frac{g(x)}{x} dx &= \int_1^3 \frac{1}{x} dx - \int_2^3 \frac{1}{x} dx &= \ln \left( \frac{4}{3} \right) \end{align*} ---------- We will now prove that \[ \int_1^3 \frac{g(x) - f(x)}{x} dx \ge 0 \] which proves the desired bound. Indeed, we have \begin{align*} \frac{1 - f(x)}{x} - \frac{1 - f(x)}{2} = \frac{1 - f(x)}{2x} (2 - x) \ge 0 \ \text{when } 1 \le x < 2 \frac{-1-f(x)}{x} - \frac{-1-f(x)}{2} = \frac{-1-f(x)}{2x} (2 - x) \ge 0 \ \text{when } 2 < x \le 3 \end{align*} Using the fact that $\int_u^v f(x) dx \le \int_u^v g(x) dx$ where $f(x) \le g(x)$ for all $x \in [u,v]$ and $f,g$ are both integrable functions in the interval $[u,v]$ , we have \begin{align*} \int_1^3 \frac{g(x) - f(x)}{x} dx &= \int_1^2 \frac{1 - f(x)}{x} dx + \int_2^3 \frac{-1-f(x)}{x} dx &\ge \int_1^2 \frac{1 - f(x)}{2} dx + \int_2^3 \frac{-1 - f(x)}{2} dx &= - \frac{1}{2} \int_{1}^{3} f(x) dx &= 0 \end{align*} Therefore, \[ \int_1^3 \frac{g(x) - f(x)}{x} dx \ge 0 \implies \int_1^3 \frac{f(x)}{x} dx \le \ln \left( \frac{4}{3} \right) \]

The maximum value of  $\int_1^3\frac{f(x)}x\,dx$  is  $\ln\left(\frac43\right),$  and this maximum is achieved.

(Note that there is an implicit hypothesis here that  $f$  must be an integrable function.)

Since  $\int_1^3\frac{f(x)}2\,dx=0,$  we can write
\begin{align*}\left|\int_1^3\frac{f(x)}x\,dx\right|&=\left|\int_1^3\frac{f(x)}x\,dx -\int_1^3\frac{f(x)}2\,dx\right|
&=\left|\int_1^3 f(x)\left(\frac1x-\frac12\right)\,dx\right|
&\le \int_1^3|f(x)|\,\left|\frac1x-\frac12\right|\,dx
&\le \int_1^31\cdot\left|\frac1x-\frac12\right|\,dx
&=\int_1^2\frac1x-\frac12\,dx+\int_2^3\frac12-\frac1x\,dx
&=\ln 2-\frac12+\frac12-\ln 3+\ln 2=\ln\left(\frac43\right)\end{align*}
We then note that we can achieve this maximum by letting  $f(x)=1$  for  $1\le x<2$  and  $f(x)=-1$  for  $2<x\le 3.$  (It doesn't matter what we set  $f(2)$  equal to.)

We could have repeated that argument with  $\frac1a$  instead of  $\frac12.$  We would get that\[\left|\int_1^3\frac{f(x)}x\,dx\right|\le\ln\left(\frac{a^2}3\right)+\frac4a-2\]
But as a function of  $a,$  this has a minimum for  $a=2,$  so setting  $a=2$  was the strongest thing we could have done.

\] where we just added  $1/2$  to each side, and noted that  $\int_2^3 1/2dx = \int_1^2 1/2dx = 1/2$ . But we can recognize that on  $[2,3]$ ,  $f(x) + 1= f(x) - g(x)$ , and on  $[1,2)$ ,  $1 - f(x) = g(x) - f(x)$ , so
\[

\] But since on  $[2,3]$ ,  $1/x \leq 1/2$  and  $f(x) -g(x) =f(x) + 1  \geq 0$  and on  $[1,2)$ ,  $1/x \geq 1/2$  and  $g(x) - f(x) = 1 - f(x) \geq 0$  we have that

\[
\int_1^3 \frac{f(x)}{x} dx \leq \int_1^3 \frac{g(x)}{x} dx = 2 \ln(2) - \ln(3).
\]

Thus the maximum the integral can achieve is:

stem_md: Let  $A$  be an  $m\times n$  matrix with rational entries. Suppose that there are at least  $m+n$  distinct prime numbers among the absolute values of the entries of  $A.$  Show that the rank of  $A$  is at least  $2.$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $Q$  be a set of entries in  $A$  such that their absolute values form  $m+n$  distinct primes. Assume that  $rank(A) \le 1$ . Then each pair of rows is  $A$  must be linearly independent, so each row must be a scalar multiple of each other.

Consider a multi-graph  $G$  with vertices  $\{1,\cdots,m\}$  such that  $i \sim j$  for each positive integer  $k \in \{1,\cdots,n\}$  such that both  $A_{ik}$  and  $A_{jk}$  are in  $Q$ , and there is no  $l \in \{i+1,\cdots,j-1\}$  such that  $A_{lk}$  is in  $Q$ . Let  $R$  be the set of all such  $k \in \{1,\cdots,n\}$  that gives  $i \sim j$ .

We claim that  $G$  is a simple, acylic graph. This is because if we have edges  $i_1 \sim i_2, i_2 \sim i_3, \cdots, i_{a-1} \sim i_a$  where  $i_1 \neq i_2 \cdots \neq i_a$  and  $a \ge 2$ , there exist  $j_1,j_2,\cdots,j_{a-1} \in \{1,\cdots,n\}$  such that  $A_{i_bj_b}$  and  $A_{i_{b+1}j_b}$  are both in  $Q$ , which means each entry in row  $i_{b+1}$  must be  $F_b = \frac{A_{i_{b+1}j_b}}{A_ij_b}$  times each entry in row  $i_b$ . Therefore, each entry in row  $i_a$  must be  $B = \prod_{c=1}^{a-1} F_c$  times each entry in row  $i_1$ . However, let's say  $i_a \sim i_1$ , forming our cycle or multi-edge. This means there exists  $j_a$  such that  $A_{i_aj_a}$  and  $A_{i_1j_a}$  are both in  $Q$ . If  $a = 2$ , then we have our multi-edge case, so  $j_a \neq j_1$   and each entry in row  $i_a$  must be  $C = \frac{A_{i_aj_a}}{A_{i_1j_a}}$  times each entry in row  $i_1$ . However, we must have  $B = C$ , which is impossible as the absolute value of  $A_{i_aj_a}$  is a distinct prime from  $A_{i_aj_1}$  by construction. 

If  $a > 2$ , then if the numerator of the simplification of our expression  $B$  isn't prime,  $B$  can never equal to  $C$  as the numerator of  $C$  is prime. Therefore, the numerator of  $B$  must be prime, and if we write  $B = \frac{A_{i_2j_1} \cdots A_{i_aj_{a-1}}}{A_{i_1j_1} \cdots A_{i_{a-1}b_{a-1}}}$ , since each of these  $A_{ij}$  entries are absolutely distinct primes in  $Q$ , we need  $(a-2)$  entries  $E$  in the numerator of  $B$  to be canceled with  $(a-2)$  entries in the denominator of  $B$ . These entries in  $E$  correspond to  $A_{i_2j_1},\cdots,A_{i_{a-1}j_{a-2}}$ , which correspond to the  $A_{i_2j_2},\cdots,A_{i_{a-1}j_{a-1}}$  entries in the denominator, as each entry in the denominator is in a different row. We cannot have  $A_{i_aj_{a-1}}$  be in  $E$  because no entry in the denominator is in the  $i_a$ th row, so we end up with  $B = \frac{A_{i_aj_{a-1}}}{A_{i_1j_1}}$ . Since the entries in  $E$  got cancelled out, we must have  $j_1 = j_2 = \cdots = j_{a-1}$  in order for  $A_{i_2j_1} = A_{i_2j_2}, \cdots, A_{i_{a-1}j_{a-2}} = A_{i_{a-1}j_{a-1}}$ . So  $B = \frac{A_{i_aj_1}}{A_{i_1j_1}}$ , and this can only equal to  $C$  if  $j_1 = j_a$ . However, this cannot happen, because for the edges  $i_1 \sim i_2, \cdots, i_{a-1} \sim i_a$  to form, we must have either  $i_1 < i_2 < \cdots < i_a$  or  $i_1 > i_2 > \cdots > i_a$ , so there exists a positive integer  $i_l$  between  $i_1$  and  $i_a$  exclusive such that  $A_{i_li_1} \in Q$ , contradicting  $i_1 \sim i_a$ . 

So  $G$  has at max  $(m-1)$  edges. Now for each  $k \in R$ , consider the longest chain of edges  $i_1 \sim i_2, \cdots, i_{a_k} \sim i_{a_{k+1}}$ , whose vertices correspond to entries  $A_{i_1k},\cdots,A_{i_{a_k+1}k}$  as they all lie on column  $k$ , so there are  $a_k+1$  total entries in  $Q$  in column  $k$ . No more entries in column  $k$  exist, or we can form another edge between the row of that entry and another row. So among these columns  $k$ , we have  $\sum_{k \in R} (a_k+1) = k + \sum_{k \in R} a_k \le k + (m-1)$  entries. Now among the  $(n-k)$  other columns, we can have at max one entry in  $Q$  in them, or else there is an edge in that column. So in total, we have at max  $k + (m-1) + (n-k) = m + n - 1$  entries in  $Q$  in our matrix, contradicting  $|Q| = m+n$ .</details>

I spent a bit of time dissecting the problem, and I got the following solution. Consider all prime factors of the numerators and denominators  $p_1,...,p_N$ . Then each rational number in the matrix can be uniquely represented by the exponents (positive or negative) the  $p_i$  in its reduced form. Thus each element of the matrix is equivalent to one in  $\Bbb{Z}^N$ . The fact that there are at least  $m+n$  primes in the matrix translates in the fact that there are at least  $m+n$  elements of the form  $(0,0...,1,...,0)$  in the vector form of the matrix, with  $1$  on different positions. Thus, the dimension of the vector space (over  $\Bbb{Q}$ ) spanned by the vectors in the matrix is at least  $m+n$ .

Suppose that  $A$  has rank  $1$ . Then  $A=(a_{i,j})=(b_ic_j)$ , and thus, the vectorized form of  $A$  has the form
\[ \begin{pmatrix} x_1+y_1 & x_1+y_2 & ... & x_1+y_n 
x_2+y_1 & x_2+y_2 & ... & x_2+y_n 
...& ... & ... & ... 
x_m+y_1 & x_m+y_2 & ... & x_m+y_n  
 \end{pmatrix}\]
It can easily be seen that the dimension of the space generated by elements of such a matrix is at most  $m+n-1$ . (Consider the  $1 \times 1$  case, then note that adding a line/column increases the dimension with at most  $1$ ). This contradiction shows that the rank of  $A$  is at least  $2$ .

stem_md: Show that for each positive integer  $n,$  all the roots of the polynomial \[\sum_{k=0}^n 2^{k(n-k)}x^k\] are real numbers.
solution_md: We can check $n \leq 2$ by \begin{align*} P_1(x) &= 1 + x, P_2(x) &= 1 + 2x + x^2 = (1+x)^2, \end{align*} which is the desired result. We show $n \geq 3$ below. Define a new polynomial \[ Q_n(x) = P_n(-x/2^n) = \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k x^k 2^{-k^2}, \] which has the same number of roots as $P_n$ . The goal will be to guarantee $n$ roots by the intermediate value theorem. Consider substituting $x = 2^{2m}$ for $m = 0, \ldots, n$ ; we have \[ f_n(m) \coloneqq 2^{-m^2} Q_n(2^m) = \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k 2^{-(k-m)^2}. \]**Claim:** We claim $f_n(m)$ has the same sign as $(-1)^m$ , for each $m = 0, 1, \ldots, n$ . *Proof.* If $m \in \{0, 1, n-1, n\}$ then the $k=m$ term will be dominant. Otherwise, the $k \in \{m-1, m, m+1\}$ terms will all cancel, and the $k \in \{m-2, m+2\}$ term(s) will be dominant. In either case, $f_n(m)$ has the same sign as $(-1)^m$ . $\square$ We are done by IVT on the intervals $[1, 2]$ , $[2, 4]$ , \ldots, $[2^{n-1}, 2^n]$ for $Q_n$ . $\blacksquare$

Motivation and contextI think here's a conceptual way to think about this problem: $\sum_{k=0}^{n} 2^{k(n-k)} x^k = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{(2^n x)^k}{2^{k^2}} = f_n(2^n x)$ , where $f_n(x) := \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{x^k}{2^{k^2}}$ is the $n$ th partial sum of the (a priori formal) power series $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{x^k}{2^{k^2}}$ . Of course $f_n(2^n x)$ has the same number of real roots as $f_n(x)$ , but I feel $f_n$ is much easier to think about! The intuition is that the denominators $2^{k^2}$ grow quickly. So vaguely, we should expect that adding a $\frac{x^n}{2^{n^2}}$ term in the $n$ th step (to get $f_n$ ) ``vertically shifts the graph of $f_{n-1}$ only a bit, if $|x|$ is not too large'' or ``shifts the real roots of $f_{n-1}$ only a little bit''---there should be the same number of real roots, plus an additional one due to (IVT and) behavior as $x\to\pm\infty$ (since all coefficients are positive, only $x\to-\infty$ contributes). (It's also helpful to try sketching a graph.) With this intuition in hand, it seems reasonable to try to find a sequence of reals $\alpha_0 > \alpha_1 > \alpha_2 > \cdots \to \infty$ such that for every $n$ , the $f_n(\alpha_i)$ (restricted to $i \le n$ ) alternate in sign; then we'll be done by IVT. Let's choose the $\alpha_i$ in order. The idea is that `` $f_j,f_{j+1},f_{j+2},\ldots$ should behave approximately the same at $x = \alpha_j$ '' (in particular they should have the same sign). We more or less want the $\frac{\alpha_j^j}{2^{j^2}}$ term to dominate (in absolute value) both the ``first $j$ pre-existing early terms'' as well as the ``error terms after $j$ ''. So for simplicity, take $\alpha_j = -2^e$ for some $e\in\mathbb{R}$ to be determined; then we want $2^{ei} / 2^{i^2} = 2^{i(e-i)}$ to be maximized at $i = j$ . So of course, we just take $e = 2j$ (by AM-GM). The rest is details; it turns out that the growth of $2^{k^2}$ is fast enough (among other less important things) for everything to work. (If the growth were, say, $2^{k^3}$ , I think it would be strictly easier to work out the details.) [Incidentally, the intuition behind the $\frac{x^n}{2^{n^2}}$ term's ``not affecting $f_{n-1}$ much for small $x$ '' also appears in many other settings, notably the sister theorems of [Weierstrass factorization theorem](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weierstrass_factorization_theorem) and [Mittag-Leffler's theorem](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mittag-Leffler%27s_theorem) in complex analysis. [In fact, the idea can be abstracted to the construction of ``inverse limits'' in homological algebra](http://mathoverflow.net/q/14717/25123): see [Mittag-Leffler condition on Wikipedia](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_limit#Mittag-Leffler_condition).] See also a blog post by HroK on ``Real roots and interlacing'' for more on the most common occurrences of ``all real roots'': http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/blog/73270

stem_md:
In the 75th Annual Putnam Games, participants compete at mathematical games. Patniss and Keeta play a game in which they take turns choosing an element from the group of invertible  $n\times n$  matrices with entries in the field  $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$  of integers modulo  $p,$  where  $n$  is a fixed positive integer and  $p$  is a fixed prime number. The rules of the game are:

(1) A player cannot choose an element that has been chosen by either player on any previous turn.

(2) A player can only choose an element that commutes with all previously chosen elements.

(3) A player who cannot choose an element on his/her turn loses the game.

Patniss takes the first turn. Which player has a winning strategy?
solution_md:
A quick sketch of a proof:

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>p odd: Have the second player respond to the matrix  $A$  by the matrix  $-A$ . He wins.

p even: Invertible  $n\times n$  matrices over  $F_2$  correspond to  $F_2$ -linear automorphisms of  $F_{2^n}$ ; each element of  $F_{2^n}^{\times}$  gives such an automorphism, given by multiplication by that element. Take a primtive root and have the first player play that as her first move. The set of matrices in the final game state must be the matrices corresponding to  $F_{2^n}^{\times}$ , which has odd size, so the first player wins.</details>

Does anyone have anything systematic about this game being played on an arbitrary finite group (not just one of these specific matrix groups)? It's clear that the end state of the game is a maximal abelian subgroup. That leads to some cheap results:

If the group is abelian, then the only issue is whether the order of the group is odd or even, and there is no strategy.

If the order of the group is odd, then the first player wins by playing randomly (no strategy).

If the order of the group is a power of two, the the second player wins by playing randomly (no strategy).

If for any other reason, all maximal abelian subgroups have even order, then the second player wins, with no strategy.

So it comes down to this: in a group of even order with an odd order maximal abelian subgroup, can the first player direct play to this subgroup or not?

Player 2 wins as soon as she plays any element of even order, so player 1 wins if she can exclude all such elements on her first turn. One way to characterize the problem is that player 2 wins iff the group is the union of the centralizers of its order 2 elements. For example, if G is any even-order group (including when G is a first-player win), G \times G is a second player win. 

One example of an even-order group that is a first-player win is the group of symmetries of the regular (2n+1)-gon.

stem_md: Let  $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$  be a function for which there exists a constant  $K>0$  such that  $|f(x)-f(y)|\le K|x-y|$  for all  $x,y\in [0,1].$  Suppose also that for each rational number  $r\in [0,1],$  there exist integers  $a$  and  $b$  such that  $f(r)=a+br.$  Prove that there exist finitely many intervals  $I_1,\dots,I_n$  such that  $f$  is a linear function on each  $I_i$  and  $[0,1]=\bigcup_{i=1}^nI_i.$
solution_md: Consider removing all reduced fractions whose denominators are at most $2K+5$ from $[0,1]$ . This splits $[0,1]$ into a finite number of disjoint open intervals; now let $I_1,\ldots,I_n$ be their closures. I claim that this works. Consider only the elements of one of the open intervals $I$ , which only has fractions with denominator greater than $2K+5$ . We now have the following claim.**Claim:** Let $\tfrac{a}{b}$ and $\tfrac{c}{d}$ be rationals with $b,d>2K+5$ and $|ad-bc|=1$ . Let $f(\tfrac{a}{b})=u\tfrac{a}{b}+v$ with $u \in [-\tfrac{b}{2},\tfrac{b}{2})$ ; then $f(\tfrac{c}{d})=u\tfrac{a}{b}+v$ as well, and $|u| \leq K$ . Proof: Observe that $\tfrac{a}{b}-\tfrac{c}{d}=\pm \tfrac{1}{bd}$ . First note that every number of the form $u'\tfrac{a}{b}+v'$ can be written uniquely as such with $u' \in [-\tfrac{b}{2},\tfrac{b}{2})$ . Now $|f(\tfrac{a}{b})-(u\tfrac{c}{d}+v)|=u|\tfrac{a}{b}-\tfrac{c}{d}|$ . On the other hand the closest number of the form $u'\tfrac{c}{d}+v'$ to $u\tfrac{c}{d}+v$ differs from it by an absolute distance of $\tfrac{1}{d}=b|\tfrac{a}{b}-\tfrac{c}{d}|$ . However no points in $[-\tfrac{b}{2},\tfrac{b}{2})$ lie outside a distance of $b$ from $u$ , so $f(\tfrac{c}{d})=u\tfrac{c}{d}+v$ is the only possibility that satisfies $$ \frac{f(\frac{a}{b})-f(\frac{c}{d})}{\frac{a}{b}-\frac{c}{d}} \in \left[-\frac{b}{2},\frac{b}{2}\right) \subset [-K,K], $$ so it must be the case. Furthermore this means we must have $u \in [-K,K]$ as well. $\blacksquare$ Now consider some $n>2K+5$ and take the portion of the $n$ -th Farey sequence that lies in $I$ . Note that adjacent elements of this sequence satisfy the $|ad-bc|$ hypothesis in the claim, and since there's at most one representation of any number as $ur+v$ with $|u| \leq K$ for any fixed $r \in I$ —because differing representations must have $u$ differing by more than $2K+5$ —we get that there exists $u,v$ with $|u| \leq K$ such that $f(r)=ur+v$ for all elements of this sequence, i.e. $f$ is linear on it. By sending $n \to \infty$ we get that $f$ is linear on $I \cap \mathbb{Q}$ , and since $f$ is continuous (since it's Lipschitz) it must be linear on $I$ and hence also linear on the closure of $I$ , which is some $I_k$ . Since this is true for all finitely many closed $I_k$ we are done. $\blacksquare$

Outline (?):

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>We use Farey sequences; i.e. we start with {0/1,1/1} and we iteratively add mediants (mediant of a/b and c/d is (a+c)/(b+d)). Some facts about Farey sequences: 1) every rational number between 0 and 1 appears in the sequence, 2) two adjacent fractions at any iteration a/b and c/d differ by 1/bd, and 3) at the Kth iteration, the sum of the denominators of any two adjacent fractions is at least K.

2) is proven by induction. (a+c)/(b+d)-a/b = (ab+bc-ab-ad)/((b+d)b)=(bc-ad)/((b+d)b) but bc-ad = 1 by inductive hypothesis.
3) is also induction, looking at how the mediant is defined.

2) is extremely important in the proof: the second condition basically states that the function at any rational number evaluates to another rational number with a denominator dividing the original rational number. What this means is that the "slope" of any two consecutive rational numbers in our Farey sequence is integral. Furthermore, we can look at what happens to the mediant. Either it lies on the line, it goes over the line, or it goes below the line. If it goes over the line, f((a+c)/(b+d)) must exceed the line by at least 1/(b+d). Then the slope to f(a/b) is increased by d, and the slope to f(c/d) decreased by b; conversely if it goes under the line, the slope to f(a/b) is decreased by d and f(c/d) increased by b.

Now consider the 100Kth Farey sequence. Every mediant must lie on the line of the adjacent fractions or else the slope will go out of bounds (as per condition #1) on one of the two sides. Thus all of the rationals must fall in a finite number of line segments. You can handle the reals because the rationals are dense so we're done.</details>

Here is a low-powered solution that doesn't use differentiability. Let  $N \geq 8K+1000$  be a fixed integer, and let  $\varepsilon = N^{-1}$ .**Lemma 1.**  $f$  is linear on  $[0, \varepsilon]$ . Analagously,  $f$  is linear on  $[1-\varepsilon, 1]$ .

*Proof:* Shift so that  $f(0) = 0$ . Note that for  $n \geq N$ ,  $f(1/n) = C_n/n$  for some  $|C_n| \leq K$ . On the other hand, we have \[
    \frac{K}{n(n+1)} \geq \left| f\left(\frac 1n \right) - f\left(\frac 1{n+1}\right)\right| = \left| \frac{C_n}{n} - \frac{C_{n+1}}{n+1}\right| \geq \frac{|C_n - C_{n+1}|}{n} - \frac{|C_{n+1}|}{n(n+1)}.
\]
So, \[
    \frac{2K}{n+1} \geq |C_n - C_{n+1}|, 
\]
but  $n+1 \geq 8K+1001 > 2K$ , so  $C_n = C_{n+1}$ , and so  $C = C_N = C_{N+1} = \cdots$  for some constant  $C$ . Now, call  $r$  *valid* if  $f(r) = Cr$ . Then, we know that  $\frac{1}{N}, \frac{1}{N+1}, \ldots$  are valid. We will shoow all  $r = \frac{a}{b} \leq \varepsilon$  are valid, by induction on  $a$  ( $a = 1$  is clear). 

Say  $r = \frac{a}{b} \leq \varepsilon$  for  $a \geq 2$ . Then, let  $c$  be minimal such that  $\frac{a-1}{c} \leq \frac{a}{b}$ , i.e. \[
    c = \left\lceil b\cdot \frac{a-1}{a}\right\rceil \leq b,
\]
and \[
    b\leq \frac{a}{a-1} \cdot c \leq 2c.
\]
Since  $s = \frac{a-1}{c} \leq r \leq \varepsilon$ ,  $s$  is good by induction. On the other hand, \[
    r-s \leq \frac{a-1}{c-1} - \frac{a-1}{c} = \frac{a-1}{c(c-1)} \leq \frac{a}{c^2}.
\]
In particular, we note that if  $f(r) = \frac{t}{b}$ , then \[
    K|r-s| \geq |f(r) - f(s)| \geq \frac{|aC-t|}{b} -C|r-s|.
\]
In particular, \[
    |aC-t| \leq 2bK|r-s| \leq \frac{2abK}{c^2} \leq \frac{4aK}{c}.
\]
But  $\frac{a}{c} \leq \frac{2(a-1)}{c} \leq 2\varepsilon$ , so \[
    |aC-t| \leq 8K\varepsilon < 1,
\]
so  $t = aC$  indeed. Thus  $f(r) = Cr$  for all rationals in  $[0, \varepsilon]$ , which by density implies that  $f$  is linear on  $[0, \varepsilon]$ .  $\Box$ **Lemma 2.** Let  $r = \frac{a}{b}$  be rational. Then,  $f$  is linear on  $\left[r, r + \frac{\varepsilon}{b}\right]$  and  $\left[r - \frac{\varepsilon}{b}, r\right]$ .

*Proof:* By symmetry we will just show that  $f$  is linear on the first interval. Define \[
    g(x) = bf(x-r), 
\]
which is Lipschitz with Lipschitz constant  $bK$  and satisfies the other condition as well. Then, by following the argument above, we get that  $g$  is linear on  $[0, (8bK+1000)^{-1}]$ , and  $\frac{1}{8bK+1000} \geq \frac{\varepsilon}{b}$ .  $\Box$ **Lemma 3.** Let  $0 < x < 1$  be arbitrary. Then,  $f$  is linear on  $[x, x-\varepsilon_x]$  and  $[x, x+\varepsilon_x]$  for some  $\varepsilon_x > 0$ .

*Proof:* If  $x$  is rational we are done by above. Else, we claim there is a rational  $r = \frac{a}{b}$  such that \[
    |x-r| < \frac{\varepsilon}{b}.
\]
Indeed, we can just take rational approximations of  $x$  that are within  $O(b^{-2})$ .  $\Box$ Now, call an open set  $A\subset [0,1]$  *allowable* if  $f$  is piecewise linear on  $A$  with at most two pieces. It is clear that  $[0, 1]$  can be covered with allowable sets, namely  $[0, \varepsilon/2)$ ,  $(1-\varepsilon/2, 1]$ , and  $(x-\varepsilon_x/2, x+\varepsilon_x/2)$ .

Taking a finite subcover, and invoking the fact that each allowable set is the union of at most 2 intervals on which  $f$  is linear, we conclude that  $[0, 1]$  is the union of some intervals, on each of which  $f$  is linear.

stem_md:
Let  $A,B\in M_n(C)$  be two square matrices satisfying  $A^2+B^2 = 2AB$ .

1.Prove that  $\det(AB-BA)=0$ .
2.If  $rank(A-B)=1$ , then prove that  $AB=BA$ .
solution_md:
Here's a different solution:
Write  $A=B+C$ . The given condition becomes  $BC+C^2=CB$ Note that  $BC^{k+1}+C^{k+2}=CBC^k$ , for all integers  $k \geq 0$ . Taking trace and noting that  $tr(BC^{k+1})=tr(BC^kC)=tr(CBC^k)$ , we get  $tr(C^k)=0$ , for all  $k \geq 2$ , so  $C$  is nilpotent. Now the problem becomes easy:
1. Since  $AB-BA=CB-BC=C^2$ , and  $C$  is nilpotent (hence singular), we are done
2.Since  $C$  is nilpotent,  $tr(C)=0$ , and  $rank(C)=1$  implies  $C^2=tr(C)C=O_n$ , so  $BC=CB$  which is equivalent to  $AB=BA$ .

stem_md: Find x, y, z  $\in Z $  $x^2+y^2+z^2=2^n(x+y+z)$  $ n\in N$
solution_md: If  $n\ge 2$ , then  $x^2+y^2+z^2\equiv 0\pmod{4}$ . Squares are  $0$  or  $1$  mod  $4$  because, e.g.,  $(2h+1)^2=4(h^2+h)+1$ ,  $(2h)^2=4h^2$ ,  $h\in\mathbb Z$ . We get  $x=2x_1$ ,  $y=2y_1$ ,  $z=2z_1$ ,  $x_1,y_1,z_1\in\mathbb Z$ .  $x_1^2+y_1^2+z_1^2=2^{n-1}(x_1+y_1+z_1)$ . If  $n-1\ge 2$ , then  $x_1=2x_2$ , etc.,  $x_2^2+y_2^2+z_2^2=2^{n-2}(x_2+y_2+z_2)$ , ... Continue this until you get  $x_k^2+y_k^2+z_k^2=2(x_k+y_k+z_k)$ . Then  $x_k^2+y_k^2+z_k^2\equiv 0\pmod{2}$ , also  $a^2\equiv a\pmod{2}$  for all  $a\in\mathbb Z$ , so  $x_k^2\equiv x_k\pmod{2}$ , etc., so  $x_k+y_k+z_k\equiv 0\pmod{2}$ , so  $4\mid 2(x_k+y_k+z_k)$ , so  $x_k^2+y_k^2+z_k^2\equiv 0\pmod{4}$ , so  $x_k=2x_{k+1}$ ,  $y_k=2y_{k+1}$ ,  $z_k=2z_{k+1}$ , so  $x_{k+1}^2+y_{k+1}^2+z_{k+1}^2=x_{k+1}+y_{k+1}+z_{k+1}$ . We have  $x_{k+1}^2\ge x_{k+1}$ ,  $y_{k+1}^2\ge y_{k+1}$ ,  $z_{k+1}^2\ge z_{k+1}$ , so  $x_{k+1}^2+y_{k+1}^2+z_{k+1}^2\ge x_{k+1}+y_{k+1}+z_{k+1}$  and equality holds if and only if  $x_{k+1}\in\{0,1\}$  and  $y_{k+1}\in\{0,1\}$  and  $z_{k+1}\in\{0,1\}$ . If  $n=1$  or  $n=0$ , then it's similar. We get that  $\exists$   $m\ge 0$ ,  $m\in\mathbb Z$  such that  $x\in\{0,2^m\}$ ,  $y\in\{0,2^m\}$ ,  $z\in\{0,2^m\}$ . Checking cases  $x=y=z=2^m$ ,  $x=0$ ,  $y=z=2^m$ ,  $x=y=0$ ,  $z=2^m$ ,  $x=y=z=0$  gives that  $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0)$  is a solution and if  $(x,y,z)\neq (0,0,0)$ , then  $m=n$ . All the solutions are  $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0)$ ,  $(0,0,2^n)$ ,  $(0,2^n,2^n)$ ,  $(2^n,2^n,2^n)$  for all  $n\in\mathbb N$  and permutations.

stem_md: Let  $ a $  be an odd natural that is not a perfect square, and  $ m,n\in\mathbb{N} . $  Then**a)**  $ \left\{ m\left( a+\sqrt a \right) \right\}\neq\left\{ n\left( a-\sqrt a \right) \right\} $ **b)**  $ \left[ m\left( a+\sqrt a \right) \right]\neq\left[ n\left( a-\sqrt a \right) \right] $ Here,  $ \{\},[] $  denotes the fractionary, respectively the integer part.
solution_md: $a)$  Suppose  $\left\{ m\left( a+\sqrt a \right) \right\}=\left\{ n\left( a-\sqrt a \right) \right\}$ . This is equivalent to  $\left\{ m\sqrt a \right\}=\left\{ -n\sqrt a \right\}$  so  $m\sqrt a -(-n\sqrt a)=(m+n)\sqrt a\in \mathbb{Z}$  which is an obvious contradiction. $b)$  Suppose  $\lfloor m\left( a+\sqrt a \right) \rfloor=\lfloor n\left( a-\sqrt a \right) \rfloor.$  Well let \[k=\lfloor m\left( a+\sqrt a \right) \rfloor=\lfloor n\left( a-\sqrt a \right) \rfloor.\] Using the properties of the floor function, we have \[k<m\left( a+\sqrt a \right)<k+1\text{ and }k<n\left( a-\sqrt a \right)<k+1\] which, dividing by  $a+\sqrt a$  and  $a-\sqrt a$  respectively and adding, we get \[\frac{k}{\frac{a-1}{2}}=\frac{2ak}{a^2-a}=\frac{k}{a+\sqrt a}+\frac{k}{a-\sqrt{a}}<m+n<\frac{k+1}{a+\sqrt a}+\frac{k+1}{a-\sqrt{a}}=\frac{2a(k+1)}{a^2-a}=\frac{k+1}{\frac{a-1}{2}}\] which is equivalent to \[k<\frac{a-1}{2}(m+n)<k+1\] which is a contradiction, because  $a$  is odd, so  $\frac{a-1}{2}(m+n)$  is an integer but so is  $k$ .

stem_md: Let be a function  $ f:\mathbb{N}\longrightarrow\mathbb{N} $  satisfying  $ \text{(i)} f(1)=1 $  $ \text{(ii)} f(p)=1+f(p-1), $  for any prime  $ p $  $ \text{(iii)} f(p_1p_2\cdots p_u)=f(p_1)+f(p_2)+\cdots f(p_u), $  for any natural number  $ u $  and any primes  $ p_1,p_2,\ldots ,p_u. $ Show that  $ 2^{f(n)}\le n^3\le 3^{f(n)}, $  for any natural  $ n\ge 2. $
solution_md: Note that we're being asked to prove that $3\log_{3}{n} \leq f(n) \leq 3\log_{2}{n}$ . First, we'll show that this holds for any prime number, to do so we'll use induction on the $n$ 'th prime number. It is trivial to see that this holds for primes $p\leq 7$ , so we'll prove it for $p\geq 11$ . So, assume that for $p_1,p_2,\dots ,p_{n-1}$ the result holds. Lemma. The result holds for all combinations of $p_1,p_2, \dots, p_{n-1}$ . Proof. Let $n=\prod_{i=1}^{n-1} p_{i}^{k_i}$ , using the third condition we have that \begin{align*} f(n) & =\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} k_i f(p_i)\leq 3\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} k_i\log_{2}{p_i}=3\log_{2}{n} \;\; \text{and} f(n) & =\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} k_i f(p_i)\geq 3\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} k_i\log_{3}{p_i}=3\log_{3}{n}. \end{align*} which proves the lemma. $\blacksquare$ Now, we'll prove that the inequalities hold for $p_n$ . Note that by the second condition, and since the result holds for $f(p_n-1)$ because all divisors of $p_n-1$ are less than $p_n$ we have that $$ f(p_n)=1+f(p_n-1)\geq 1+3\log_{3}(p_n-1) \geq3 \log_{3}(p_n) $$ beacuse $\left(\frac{p_n}{p_n-1}\right)^3\leq 3$ holds for $p_n \geq 11$ . Also, since that all prime divisors of $p_n+1$ are less than $p_n$ the result holds for $f(p_n+1)$ , so using the second condition we get $$ f(p_n)=f(p_n+1)-1\leq 3\log_{2}(p_n+1)-1 \leq 3\log_{2}(p_n) $$ because $\left(\frac{p_n+1}{p_n}\right)^3 \leq 2$ for $p_n \geq 11$ , which shows that the result holds for $p_n$ too, hence by induction hypothesis the problem statement holds for all prime numbers. Let $n=\prod_{i=1}^{\ell} p_{i}^{k_i}$ , we have that \begin{align*} f(n) & =\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} k_i f(p_i)\leq 3\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} k_i\log_{2}{p_i}=3\log_{2}{n} \;\; \text{and} f(n) & =\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} k_i f(p_i)\geq 3\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} k_i\log_{3}{p_i}=3\log_{3}{n}. \end{align*} which proves the problem for all $n \geq 2$ . $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Let  $ n $  be a natural number, and  $ A $  the set of the first  $ n $  natural numbers. Find the number of nondecreasing functions  $ f:A\longrightarrow A $  that have the property   $$  x,y\in A\implies |f(x)-f(y)|\le |x-y|.  $$
solution_md:
So certainly  $f(x+1) \in \{f(x),f(x)+1\}$ . On the other hand, every such function satisfies the condition.
Suppose that  $f(n)-f(1)=k$ . Then we have  $\binom{n-1}{k}$  choices of where the increments should be and  $n-k$  choices of  $f(1)$  yielding the result
\[\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (n-k) \binom{n-1}{k}=n2^{n-1}-(n-1)2^{n-2}\]

stem_md: Let  $ A\in\mathcal{M}_4\left(\mathbb{R}\right) $  be an invertible matrix whose trace is equal to the trace of its adjugate, which is nonzero. Show that  $ A^2+I $  is singular if and only if there exists a nonzero matrix in  $ \mathcal{M}_4\left( \mathbb{R} \right) $  that anti-commutes with it.
solution_md:
I'll take "inversable" as meaning "invertible".

Let  $a={\rm tr}(A),\ d=\det(A)$ , then the hypothesis are  $a,d\neq0,$  and the characteristic polynomial of  $A$  is  $t^4-at^3+bt^2-at+d$  for some  $b\in{\mathbb R}.$ Suppose there exists  $B\in\mathcal{M}_4(\mathbb{R})$  such that  $B\neq0$  and  $AB=-BA.$ Then  $B$  anti-commutes with all the odd powers of  $A$ , while it commutes with all the even powers of  $A.$  Note that, on a filed of characteristic different from 2, if a matrix  $M$  commutes and anti-commutes with a matrix  $N$ , then  $MN=NM=0$  ( $MN=NM=-MN$ .)
We have  $A^4+bA^2+dI=a(A^3+A)$  so  $B$  commutes with  $A^4+bA^2+dI$  and anti-commutes with  $a(A^3+A)$ , thus  $aA(A^2+I)B=0$ , which implies  $(A^2+I)B=0$ , since  $a\neq0$  and  $A$  is invertible.
We obtain that the image of  $B$  (which is not  $\{0\}$ ) is included in the kernel of  $A^2+I$ , which is therefore singular.

Working in the other direction, we don't need all the hypothesis, just that  $a\neq 0$ . Observe that the problem is invariant under similarity, so we may suppose  $A$  in (real) Jordan normal form.
Suppose  $A^2+I$  is singular. Then  $A^2$  has the eigenvalue -1, which implies that the (complex) spectrum of  $A$  contains  $i$  and  $-i$ . Since  $a\neq0$ , the spectrum of  $A$  can't contain only  $i$  and  $-i$ . This in turn implies that the Jordan normal form of  $A$  is of type $\begin{pmatrix}C&0 0&D\end{pmatrix}$  where  $C=\begin{pmatrix}0&1 -1&0\end{pmatrix}$  and  $D\in\mathcal{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ .
Then take  $B=\begin{pmatrix}E&0 0&0\end{pmatrix}$  with  $E=\begin{pmatrix}0&1 1&0\end{pmatrix}$ .

stem_md: For a ring  $ A, $  and an element  $ a $  of it, define  $ s_a,d_a:A\longrightarrow A, s_a(x)=ax,d_a=xa.$ **a)** Prove that if  $ A $  is finite, then  $ s_a $  is injective if and only if  $ d_a $  is injective.**b)** Give example of a ring which has an element  $ b $  for which  $ s_b $  is injective and  $ d_b $  is not, or, conversely,  $ s_b $  is not injective, but  $ d_b $  is.
solution_md: a) Observe that  $s_a$  and  $d_a$  are group endomorphisms of  $(A,+)$ .  $s_a$  is injective means that  $\ker s_a=\{0\}$  so  $a^k$  can never be  $0$ . Since  $A$  is finite, there exists nonnegative integers  $i<j$  such that  $a^i=a^j$ . Hence  $aa^{i-1}(1-a^{j-i})=(a^i(1-a^{j-i})=0$  so  $a^{i-1}(1-a^{j-i})$  (if  $i$  was equal to  $0$  we were done before this step). By induction,  $a^{j-i}=1$  so  $a$  is a unit. Then clearly  $\ker d_a=\{0\}$  so  $d_a$  is injective. The converse can be proven similarly.  $\square$

candidates:
For a) to be correct, you'll need your ring to have  $1,$  the multiplicative identity. Let me first give you a counter-example to a). Let  $R$  be any ring with  $1$  and consider  $$ A:=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}u & v  0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}: \ \ u,v \in R \right\} \subset M_2(R). $$  Of course, if you want  $A$  to be finite, choose  $R$  to be finite, e.g.  $R=\mathbb{Z}_2$ . Now, let  $a=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0  0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \in A.$  Then  $s_a$  is injective because  $s_a(x)=ax=x$  for all  $x \in A.$  But  $d_a$  is not injective because, for example, with  $x=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1  0 & 0 \end{pmatrix},$  we have  $d_a(x)=xa=0.$  

But we won't have that problem if we assume that  $A$  is finite with  $1$ . To see that, suppose  $s_a$  is injective for some  $a \in A$  and  $d_a(x)=xa=0$  for some  $x \in A.$  Since  $A$  is finite,  $a^m=a^n$  for some integers  $1 \le m < n,$  implying that  $a^m(1-a^{n-m})=0$  and hence  $1=a^{n-m}$  because  $s_a$  is injective. Since  $n-m \ge 1,$  we get from  $d_a(x)=xa=0$  that  $0=xa^{n-m}=x$  and so  $d_a$  is injective. 
Conversely, if  $d_a$  is injective, a similar argument works: since  $A$  is finite,  $a^m=a^n$  for some integers  $1 \le m < n$  and so  $(1-a^{n-m})a^m=0$  implying that  $a^{n-m}=1$  because  $d_a$  is injective. So if  $s_a(x)=ax=0,$  then  $0=a^{n-m}x=x$  proving that  $s_a$  is injective.

stem_md: Let  $ I,J $  be two intervals,  $ \varphi :J\longrightarrow\mathbb{R} $  be a continuous function whose image doesn't contain  $ 0, $  and  $ f,g:I\longrightarrow J $  be two differentiable functions such that  $ f'=\varphi\circ f,g'=\varphi\circ g $  and such that the image of  $ f-g $  contains  $ 0. $ Show that  $ f $  and  $ g $  are the same function.
solution_md:
Since  $\varphi$  is continuous and doesn't vanish we can take  $F: J \longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$  to be the antiderivative of  $1/\varphi$ . $(F \circ f)' (x) = 1, \forall x \in I \Rightarrow F(f(x))=x+a$  $(F \circ g)' (x) = 1, \forall x \in I \Rightarrow F(f(g))=x+b$ Now, because  $0 \in Im(f-g)$  we get that  $a=b$ . $F'$  doesn't vanish, which means  $\text{sgn}(F'(x))$  is constant, so  $F$  is strictly monotonic, which implies  $F$  is injective.

Since  $F(f(x))=F(g(x))$  and  $F$  is injective, we conclude that  $f=g$

stem_md: Let  $ f:[1,\infty )\longrightarrow (0,\infty ) $  be a continuous function satisfying the following properties: $ \text{(i)}\exists\lim_{x\to\infty } \frac{f(x)}{x}\in\overline{\mathbb{R}} $  $ \text{(ii)}\exists\lim_{x\to\infty } \frac{1}{x}\int_1^x f(t)dt\in\mathbb{R}. $ **a)** Show that  $ \lim_{x\to\infty } \frac{f(x)}{x}=0. $ **b)** Prove that  $ \lim_{x\to\infty } \frac{1}{x^2}\int_1^x f^2(t)dt=0. $
solution_md:
Solution (a)Considering $g(x)=\int_{1}^{x}f(t)dt$ , then we have $L=\lim_{x\to\infty } \frac{1}{x}\int_1^x f(t)dt=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\frac{d}{dx}{\int_1^x f(t)dt}}{\frac{d}{dx}x}=\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)$ so $\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=L$ , so $\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{e^xf(x)}{e^x}=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\frac{d}{dx}(e^xf(x))}{\frac{d}{dx}e^x}=\lim_{x\to\infty}(f(x)+f'(x))\Rightarrow \lim_{x\to\infty}f'(x)=L-L=0$ so we have shown that $\lim_{x\to\infty}f'(x)=0$ Now as we have $\lim_{x\to\infty}f'(x)=0$ , so given any $p>0$ , $\exists M>0$ , such that $|f'(x)|<\frac{p}{2}$ , $\forall x\ge M$ Now we have from mean value theorem $|f(x)-f(M)|=|f'(c_x)||x-M|<\frac{p}{2}x$ , $\forall x>M$ , $\exists c_x\in (M,x)$ and $|f'(c_x)|<\frac{p}{2}$ Then we have $|\frac{f(x)}{x}-\frac{f(M)}{x}|<\frac{p}{2}$ , $\forall x>M$ so $|\frac{f(x)}{x}|\le |\frac{f(x)}{x}-\frac{f(M)}{x}|+|\frac{f(M)}{x}|<2\frac{p}{2}=p$ , $\forall x>\max \{M,\frac{2}{p}|f(M)|\}$ or $|\frac{f(x)}{x}|\max \{M,\frac{2}{p}|f(M)|\}$ , Hence we have $\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{f(x)}{x}=0$
Solution (b)Now considering $\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{1}{x^2}\int_{1}^{x}f^{2}(t)dt=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\frac{d}{dx}\int_{1}^{x}f^{2}(t)dt}{\frac{d}{dx}x^2}=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{f^{2}(x)}{2x}=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\frac{d}{dx}f^{2}(x)}{\frac{d}{dx}(2x)}=\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)f'(x)$ or $\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{1}{x^2}\int_{1}^{x}f^{2}(t)dt=\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)f'(x)=0$ , as $\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=L$ and $\lim_{x\to\infty}f'(x)=0$

stem_md: Let be a finite group  $ G $  that has an element  $ a\neq 1 $  for which exists a prime number  $ p $  such that  $ x^{1+p}=a^{-1}xa, $  for all  $ x\in G. $ **a)** Prove that the order of  $ G $  is a power of  $ p. $ **b)** Show that  $ H:=\{x\in G|\text{ord} (x)=p\}\le G $  and  $ \text{ord}^2(H)>\text{ord}(G). $
solution_md:
Let  $\pi\in\mathrm{Inn}(G)$  be the inner automorphism given by  $x\mapsto a^{-1}xa=x^{1+p}$ .

a) Notice that  $g\in C_G(a)\iff\pi(g)=g\iff g^p=e$  so
\[
C_G(a)=\{g\in G\mid\pi(g)=g\}=\{g\in G\mid g^p=e\}=H.
\]
Note that  $a\in H$ . For  $g\in G$  and  $h\in H$ , we have
\[
\pi(g^{-1}hg)=(g^{-1}hg)^{1+p}=g^{-1}h^{1+p}g=g^{-1}hg
\]
so  $g^{-1}hg\in H$ . Thus  $H\trianglelefteq G$ . For  $g\in G$ , we have  $g^{1+p}=a^{-1}ga\in gH$  so  $g^p\in H$ . Hence  $g^{p^2}=e$  for all  $g\in G$ , so we are done by Cauchy's theorem.  $\square$ b) Since  $g^{p^2}=e$  for all  $g\in G$ , it follows that  $\pi^{-1}$  is given by  $x\mapsto x^{1-p}$ . Since  $\pi^{-1}$  is an automorphism, we have
\[
y^{1-p}x^{1-p}=(yx)^{1-p}=y(xy)^{-p}x\implies y^{-p}x^{-p}=(xy)^{-p}\implies x^py^p=(xy)^p
\]
for all  $x,y\in G$ . Let homomorphism  $\varphi:G\mapsto H$  be given by  $x\mapsto x^p$ . Since  $\ker\varphi=H$ , it follows that  $|G|=|H|\cdot|\mathrm{im}\ \varphi|$  so it suffices to prove that  $\mathrm{im}\ \varphi<H$ .

We claim that  $a\not\in\mathrm{im}\ \varphi$ , which finishes. Suppose FTSOC there exists  $g\in G$  such that  $g^p=a$ . Then  $ga=g^{1+p}=ag$  implies that  $g\in H$ . It follows that  $g^p=e\neq a$ , a contradiction.  $\square$

stem_md: Find all primes  $p$  and  $q$ , with  $p \le q$ , so that   $$ p (2q + 1) + q (2p + 1) = 2 (p^2 + q^2). $$
solution_md: This is equivalent to   $$ p+q=2(q-p)^2. $$  Note that   $$ p+q>0\implies q-p\neq 0\implies q>p\ge 2. $$  Now,   $$ 2(q-p) ^2\equiv 0 \pmod 2\implies p+q\equiv 0\pmod 2\implies p, q\;\text{are of same parity.} $$  Therefore, let  $q=p+2k,$  then   $$ 2p+2k=8k^2\implies p=4k^2-k=k(4k-1). $$  But since  $p$  is a prime, we must have   $$ k=1. $$  Thus,   $$ q=4k^2+k=5. $$  Hence,  $(p, q) =(3, 5)$  is the only solution.

stem_md: Let  $a,b,c\in \left( 0,\infty  \right)$ .Prove the inequality $\frac{a-\sqrt{bc}}{a+2\left( b+c \right)}+\frac{b-\sqrt{ca}}{b+2\left( c+a \right)}+\frac{c-\sqrt{ab}}{c+2\left( a+b \right)}\ge 0.$
solution_md:
Denote  $\displaystyle A = \sum \dfrac {a}{a+2(b+c)}$  and  $\displaystyle B = \sum \dfrac {\sqrt{bc}}{a+2(b+c)}$ . Then, by the (Titu version of) Cauchy-Schwarz inequality
\[A = \sum \dfrac {a}{a+2(b+c)} = \sum \dfrac {a^2}{a^2+2(ab+ca)}\geq \dfrac {\big ( \sum a \big )^2} {\sum a^2 + 4\sum bc} \geq \dfrac {3}{5},\]
since it comes to  $\displaystyle 2\sum a^2 \geq 2\sum bc$ , i.e.  $\displaystyle \sum (b-c)^2 \geq 0$ . But by the AM-GM inequality
\[B = \sum \dfrac {\sqrt{bc}}{a+2(b+c)} \leq \sum \dfrac {(b+c)/2}{a+2(b+c)} = \dfrac {1} {4}(3 - A),\]
so  $B \leq \dfrac {1} {4}\left (3 - \dfrac {3}{5}\right ) = \dfrac {3}{5}$ , therefore  $A \geq \dfrac {3}{5} \geq B$ , whence  $\boxed{A-B \geq 0}$ . Equality clearly holds if and only if  $a=b=c$ .

stem_md: Let $f$ be the function of the set of positive integers into itself, defi ned by $f(1) = 1$ , $f(2n) = f(n)$ and $f(2n + 1) = f(n) + f(n + 1)$ . Show that, for any positive integer $n$ , the number of positive odd integers m such that $f(m) = n$ is equal to the number of positive integers**less or equal to** $n$ and coprime to $n$ . [mod: the initial statement said less than $n$ , which is wrong.]
solution_md: Straightforward but nice functional equation.**Claim:** For every $n \geq 1$ , $\gcd(f(n), f(n+1)) = 1$ . *Proof:* By strong induction. We can compute $f$ manually for $n \leq 3$ . Now, \begin{align*} \gcd(f(2n), f(2n+1)) &= \gcd(f(n), f(n)+f(n+1)) = 1 \gcd(f(2n+1), f(2n+2)) &= \gcd(f(n+1), f(n)+f(n+1)) = 1. \end{align*}**Claim:** There do not exist distinct positive integers $m, n$ such that $\{f(n), f(n+1)\} = \{f(m), f(m+1)\}$ . *Proof:* Assume otherwise, and let $(m, n)$ be such a pair with $m+n$ minimal. We only check the case $(m, n) = (2m', 2n')$ ; the other parity cases follow similarly. In this case, $f(n) < f(n+1)$ and $f(m) < f(m+1)$ , so it follows that \begin{align*} f(m') = f(m) = f(n) = f(n') f(m'+1) = f(m+1)-f(m) = f(n+1) - f(n) = f(n'+1). \end{align*} So $(m', n')$ is another such pair with $m'+n' < m+n$ , contradiction. $\blacksquare$ Fix $n$ now. For any positive integer $m$ with $f(2m+1) = n$ , we must have $\{f(m), f(m+1)\} = \{n-k, k\}$ for some $\gcd(n, k) = 1$ by the first claim. There are at most $\phi(n)$ such pairs and thus $\phi(n)$ integers $m$ by the second claim, which gives the desired result.

Let  $n$  be a positive integer and let  $A_n$  respectively  $B_n$  be the set of nonnegative integers  $k<n$  such that the number of distinct prime factors of  $\gcd(n,k)$  is even  (respectively odd). Show that  $|A_n|=|B_n|$  if  $n$  is even and  $|A_n|>|B_n|$  if  $n$  is odd.

Example:  $A_{10} = \left\{ 0,1,3,7,9 \right\}$ ,  $B_{10} = \left\{ 2,4,5,6,8 \right\}$ .
solution_md:
Define the function  $f(n)=|A_n|-|B_n|$ . Obviously  $f(1)=1$ .

Let us notice that if  $n$  is a positive integer divisible by a prime  $p$ , then  $\gcd(x,n)$  and  $\gcd(x+nk,pn)$  have the same prime factors for all  $x$  and  $k$ . This means that if  $x\in X_n$  it follows that  $\{x,x+n,x+2n,...,x+(p-1)n\}\subset \{X_{np}\}$ , where  $X\in \{A,B\}$ . It immediately results that  $|A_{np}|=p|A_n|$  and  $|B_{np}|=p|B_n|$ , hence  $f(np)=pf(n)$ .

Therefore it is sufficient to prove the assertion for  $n=\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{s}p_i$ , where  $p_1,p_2,...,p_s$  are different prime numbers. Let's remark now that: $\bullet$  a number  $x$  counts in  $f(n)$  as  $\mu(d)$ , where  $d=\gcd(n,x)$  and  $\mu$  is Möbius function; $\bullet$  there are  $\varphi(\frac nd)$  numbers  $x$  that satisfy the property  $d=\gcd(x,n)$ .

We obtain  $f(n)=\displaystyle\sum_{d\mid n} \mu(d)\varphi(\frac nd)$ . (and eventually we could get using Möbius inversion formula that  $\varphi(n) =\displaystyle\sum_{d\mid n} f(d)$ ) 
Now a classical  $PIE$  argument gives us:

 \[f(p_1\cdot p_2\cdot \ldots \cdot p_s)=(p_1-2)\cdot (p_2-2)\cdot \ldots \cdot(p_s-2)\]

stem_md: Let  $n \ge 2$  be an integer. Show that there exist  $n+1$  numbers  $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{n+1} \in \mathbb{Q} \setminus \mathbb{Z}$ , so that  $\{ x_1^3 \} + \{ x_2^3 \} + \cdots + \{ x_n^3 \}=\{ x_{n+1}^3 \}$ , where  $\{ x \}$  is the fractionary part of  $x$ .
solution_md: Pick a very large  $p\equiv 2\pmod 3$ .Will be looking for numbers in the form  $x_i=\tfrac{a_{i}}{p}$ ,note that  $\{\tfrac{a_i^3}{p}\}=\tfrac{(a_i)_{p^3}}{p^3}$  ,where  $x_{p^3}$  is the residue class modulo of  $x$  modulo  $p^3$ .Let  $j$  be the generator of  $\mathbb{Z}_{p^3,\times}$  and let  $y=j^k=\left( j^{(k\cdot 3^{-1})}\right)^3$  where the equality is regarded in  $\mathbb{Z}_{p^3}$  and  $3^{-1}\equiv \frac{1}{3} \pmod{p^2(p-1)}$  (one surely exists as  $(p^2(p-1),2)=1$ ).Notice that by the previous every proper residue in  $\mathbb{Z}_{p^3}$  is a cubic one.Now  $a_i^3\equiv i\pmod {p^3}$  and note that  $LHS=\tfrac{\binom{n+2}{2}}{p^3}$  and select  $a_{n+1}\equiv \binom{n+2}{2}_{p^3}$ .Now set  $p\gg \binom{n+2}{2}$  and hence we reach the equality. $\blacksquare$ If I am not mistaken the above should be able to generalize to the existence of  $x_i$  so that :  $$ \sum_{i=1}^n \{x_i^m\}=\{x_{n+1}^m\} $$  Where  $m>1$  is an arbitrary odd number.

Let  $n \in \mathbb{N}$  and  $S_{n}$  the set of all permutations of  $\{1,2,3,...,n\}$ . For every permutation  $\sigma \in S_{n}$  denote  $I(\sigma) := \{ i: \sigma (i) \le i \}$ .
Compute the sum  $\sum_ {\sigma \in S_{n}} \frac{1}{|I(\sigma	)|} \sum_ {i \in I(\sigma)} (i+ \sigma(i))$ .
solution_md:
Draw  $n\times n$  grid in the plane with the lower left in  $(1,1)$  and the upper right in  $(n+1,n+1)$ .Now start marking points  $(i,\sigma(i))$ ,they're clearly all inside the gird.Note that  $I(\sigma)$  is exactly those points on the left side when girded is divided by the main diagonal.

Adjoin to permutation  $\sigma$  a new one  $\sigma'$  by reflecting the grid over the other diagonal.Note that :  $$ \sum_{i\in I(\sigma)} (i+\sigma(i))+\sum_{i\in I(\sigma')} (i+\sigma'(i))=2I(\sigma)(n+1) $$  as  $I(\sigma)=I(\sigma')$ .Now multiplying the above sum by two and pairing off  $(\sigma,\sigma')$  one obtains that the sum is actually  $\sum_{\sigma \in S_n} n+1=(n+1)!$ . $\blacksquare$ Just a remark,if one looks at the incidence matrix of the permutation the  $(i+\sigma(i))$  becomes the sum of sides of a rectangle made out of  $(i,\sigma(i))$  and its projections on the axes which seemed reasonably nice ,but i couldn't force a solution out of it.

A solution without Dirichlet's Theorem
Click to expandFirst we state the lemma and prove it: Lemma: Let $p$ be and odd prime, $m>1$ and $m+1$ is not divisible by $p$ then the number $m^{p^k}$ has at least $k$ distinct prime factors Proof: To prove this lemma, we have a small statement as follow: *Statement:* $m^{p^l}+1$ is not divisibly by $p$ , indeed, assume the contrary, $p|m^{p^l}+1 \rightarrow p|m^{2p^l}-1$ then $ord_{p}(m)|2p^l$ but $ord_{p}(m)|p-1$ thus $ord_{p}(m)|gcd(2p^l,p-1)=1,2$ #If $ord_{p}(m)=1$ then $p|m-1$ implies $p|m^{p^l}-1$ , but since $p|m^{p^l}+1$ then $p|2$ a contradiction! #if $ord_{p}(m)=2$ then $p|m^2-1$ implies $p|m+1$ (because if $p|m-1$ then $ord_{p}(m)=1$ a contradiction) but this is also a contradiction since we assume that $m+1$ is not divisible by $p$ __ Now, come back to our lemma, $m^{p^k}+1=(A+1)(A^{p-1}-...-A+1)$ where $A$ is $m^{p^{k-1}}$ Let $d=gcd(A+1,A^{p-1}-...-A+1)$ then $A \equiv -1 \pmod{d}$ thus $A^{p-1}-...-A+1 \equiv p \pmod{d}$ , hence $d|p$ but from above claim, we prove that $A+1=m^{p^{k-1}}+1$ is not divisible by $p$ then $d=1$ so $A+1,A^{p-1}-...+A-1$ are relatively prime, immediately, we have $A^{p-1}+...+A+1$ has at least a prime factor which doesn't occur in prime factorization of $A+1$ , and note that $A+1=m^{p^{k-1}}+1$ applying the above proof for $k-1$ times, we obtain $m^{p^k}$ has at least $k$ distinct prime factors... _________________ Come back to our problem Case 1: $m>1$ , first, for convenience, choose $n=m^t$ for which $t$ will be chosen later. Thus $m^n+n^m=m^{m^t}+m^{tm}=m^{tm}(m^{m^t-tm}+1=m^{tm}((m^m)^{m^{t-1}-t}+1)$ It suffices prove for $(m^m)^{m^{t-1}-t}+1$ that it will have $k$ distinct prime factors First, we prove there exist $t$ such that $p^k|m^{t-1}-t$ with $p$ is an odd prime and $p|m$ since $m>1$ and $m$ is an odd number $p^k|m^{t-1}-t$ simply choose $t=p^k$ thus $t-1=p^k-1>k$ then $p^k|m^{t-1}-t$ (since $p|m$ ) So, we have $m^{t-1}-t=p^k.w$ with $w$ is an integer Now, $(m^m)^{m^{t-1}-t}+1=(m^{mw})^{p^k}+1$ since $m^{mw}+1 \equiv 1 \pmod {p}$ (since $p|m)$ so $m^{mw}+1$ is not divisibly by $p$ , applying the lemma, we obtain $(m^{mw})^{p^k}+1$ has at least $k$ prime factors, *Case 2:* $m=1$ then $m^n+n^m=1+n$ this is obviously easy, simply choose $n=p_1.p_2...p_k-1$ with $p_1,...,p_k$ are distinct primes number

Let $k$ be a nonzero natural number and $m$ an odd natural number . Prove that there exist a natural number $n$ such that the number $m^n+n^m$ has at least $k$ distinct prime factors.
We first prove by induction that there exists $k$ primes $p_1,p_2,...,p_k$ ( $>m$ ) satisfying $\gcd((p_1-1)..(p_k-1),p_1p_2...p_k))=1$ , for $k=1$ it's easy, if $p_1,p_2,...,p_{k-1}$ are already found then by Dirichlet theorem we can find $p_k$ large enough ( $> \max_i\{p_i-1\}$ ) and having the form $p_k=tN+2$ where $N=p_1p_2...p_{k-1}$ , such $p_k$ is obviously the good one to finish the induction ! Now by the Chinese remainder theorem we can find $n$ satisfying the two conditions $n \equiv -1 \pmod{ p_1p_2...p_k}$ and $n\equiv 0 \pmod{(p_1-1)..(p_k-1)}$ , by Fermat's little theorem we can easily see that $m^n+n^m$ has at least $p_1...,p_k$ as a prime divisors.

This solution is similar to tahanguyen98's, but the use of Zsigmondy's Theorem makes it much shorter.

stem_md:
Let  $n$  be an integer greater than  $1$  and let  $S$  be a finite set containing more than  $n+1$  elements.Consider the collection of all sets  $A$  of subsets of  $S$  satisfying the following two conditions :**(a)** Each member of  $A$  contains at least  $n$  elements of  $S$ .**(b)** Each element of  $S$  is contained in at least  $n$  members of  $A$ .

Determine  $\max_A \min_B |B|$  , as  $B$  runs through all subsets of  $A$  whose members cover  $S$  , and  $A$  runs through the above collection.
solution_md:
We will prove, the required number is  $|S|-n$ .
Let  $\mathcal{A}$  is a set of subsets of  $S$ , satisfying (a) and (b). One can choose  $|S|-n+1$  members of  $\mathcal{A}$ , covering  $S$  as follows: first take any  $A\in \mathcal{A}$ , which covers at least  $n$  elements of  $S$ , and then for each of the remaining at most  $|S|-n$  elements, choose a set covering that element. **Claim**: There exist  $|S|-n$  members of  $\mathcal{A}$ , covering  $S$ .
*Proof*: If some member of  $\mathcal{A}$  has more than  $n$  elements, we are done in the same way as shown above. Suppose each member of  $\mathcal{A}$  consists of  $n$  elements of  $S$ . Take arbitrary  $A\in \mathcal{A}$ . Consider  $A^c=S-A$ . If some  $A' \in \mathcal{A}$  meats two or more alements of  $A^c$  we are done, so suppose  $|A'\cap A^c|=1$  for all  $A' \in \mathcal{A}, A' \neq A$ . Fix  $x\in A^c$ . According to (b), any set consisting of  $x$  plus  $n-1$  elements of  $A$  should belong to  $\mathcal{A}$ . But then, for every  $x\in A^c$ , one can choose  $A_x\in \mathcal{A}$  with  $x\in A_x$  and  $A \subset \bigcup_{x\in A^c} A_x$ , which means  $S=\bigcup_{x\in A^c} A_x$   $\blacksquare$ Therefore, we proved  $\max_A \min_B |B|\leq |S|-n$ . 
Now, consider a family  $\mathcal{A}$  of subsets of  $S$  as follows: Suppose  $S=\{1,2,\dots, m\}\, ,m\geq n+2$ . Then  $\mathcal{A} := \{ A\subset S : A= (\{1,2,\dots,n\} \setminus \{x\}) \cup \{y\}\,,\, x\in\{1,2,\dots n\}, y\in\{n+1,\dots,m\}  \}$ . Clearly, there do not exist  $m-n-1$  members of  $\mathcal{A}$  covering  $S$ , implying
\[\max_A \min_B |B| = |S|-n.\]

stem_md: Let  $ABC$  be a triangle and let  $X$ , $Y$ , $Z$  be interior points on the sides  $BC$ ,  $CA$ ,  $AB$ , respectively. Show that the magnified image of the triangle  $XYZ$  under a homothety of factor  $4$  from its centroid covers at least one of the vertices  $A$ ,  $B$ ,  $C$ .
solution_md:
We proceed with barycentric coordinates where we take  $ \triangle{XYZ}$  to be our reference triangle.  WLOG let  $ X = (1, 0, 0) $  and  $ Y = (0, 1, 0) $  and  $ Z = (0, 0, 1). $   Let the homothety with ratio  $ 4 $  centered at  $ G $  take points  $ X, Y, Z $  to points  $ X', Y', Z'. $   Since  $ G = \left(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{3}\right) $  we find that  $ X' = (3, -1, -1) $  and  $ Y' = (-1, 3, -1) $  and  $ Z' = (-1, -1, 3). $   This lets us easily compute the equations of lines  $ Y'Z', Z'X', X'Y' $  to be  $ 2x + y + z = 0 $  and  $ x + 2y + z = 0 $  and  $ x + y + 2z = 0 $  respectively. 

Assume for the sake of contradiction that points  $ A, B, C $  all lie outside  $ \triangle{X'Y'Z'}. $   Letting  $ A = (r , s, t) $  for some  $ r, s, t \in \mathbb{R} $  that satisfy  $ r + s + t = 1, $  we must have that  $ s, t > 0 $  and  $ 2r + s + t < 0. $   Now let  $ M = AY \cap X'Y' $  and  $ N = AZ \cap X'Z'. $   Since  $ C \in AM $  and  $ B \in AN $  such that  $ M $  is between  $ A $  and  $ C $  and  $ N $  is between  $ A $  ad  $ B $ , we have since  $ BC $  passes through  $ X $  that line  $ MN $  passes through  $ \triangle{XYZ}. $ Now it is easy to compute that line  $ AY $  has equation  $ rz = tx $  and line  $ AZ $  has equation  $ ry = sx $  so we find that  $ M = (r : - 2r - t : t) $  and  $ N = (r : s : -2r - s) $  so line  $ MN $  has equation  $ (3st + 2rs + 2rt + r^2)x + r(r + 2s + t)y + r(r + s + 2t)z = 0. $   Note that  $ 3st + 2rs + 2rt + r^2 = 3(st - r^2) + 2r(2r + s + t) <  3(st - r^2) < 3\left(st - \frac{(s + t)^2}{2}\right) < 0 $  and  $ r(r + 2s + t) = r(1 + s) < 0 $  and  $ r(r + s + 2t) = r(1 + t) < 0 $  which imply that point  $ X $  and segment  $ YZ $  are on the same side of  $ MN. $   This means that  $ MN $  does not pass through  $ \triangle{XYZ}, $  contradiction!
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2014 Contests/2014 Romania Team Selection Test/621876.json

stem_md: Determine all positive integers  $n$  such that all positive integers less than  $n$  and coprime to  $n$  are powers of primes.
solution_md:
Let me expand on AdithyaBhaskar's argument.  Let  $ n = \prod_{i = 1}^{\infty}p_i^{a_i} $  where  $ p_i $  is the  $ i $ th prime and the  $ a_i $  are nonnegative integers.  Let  $ r $  be the smallest positive integer for which  $ a_r = 0 $  and let  $ s $  be the second smallest positive integer for which  $ a_s = 0. $   Then since  $ \text{gcd}(p_rp_s, n) = 1 $  we must have  $ p_rp_s > n \ge \frac{1}{p_r}\prod_{i = 1}^{s - 1}p_i. $   Call this the *fundamental inequality*This means that  $ p_sp_{s - 1} > \prod_{i = 1}^{s - 2}p_i $  and a quick use of Bertrand's postulate shows that that this is true only when  $ s \le 5. $   Now, assume there existed an integer  $ t > s $  such that  $ a_t \ne 0. $   Then we would need to have  $ p_sp_{s - 1} > p_{s + 1}\prod_{i = 1}^{s - 2}p_i $  which again by Bertrand's postulate and some quick multiplication can only occur if  $ n = 5 $  or if  $ n = 14. $   Therefore, since we must have  $ n < p_rp_s \le p_4p_5 = 77 $  we can just check all  $ 76 $  cases.
 
We find that the solution is  $ \boxed{n \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 14, 18, 20, 24, 30, 42\}} $

stem_md: For every positive integer  $n$ , let  $\sigma(n)$  denote the sum of all positive divisors of  $n$  ( $1$  and  $n$ , inclusive). Show that a positive integer  $n$ , which has at most two distinct prime factors, satisfies the condition  $\sigma(n)=2n-2$   if and only if  $n=2^k(2^{k+1}+1)$ , where  $k$  is a non-negative integer and  $2^{k+1}+1$  is prime.
solution_md:
If  $n$  is a positive integer which has at most two prime divisors, then   $(1) \;\; \sigma(n) = 2n-2$ iff ${n=2^k(2^{k+1} + 1})$ , where  $k$  is an non-negative integer and  $2^{k+1} + 1$  is a prime.**Proof:** Clearly  $n \neq 1$  by (1).  Hence  $n$  has one or two prime divisors. Thus we have the following two cases:**Case 1:**  $n=p^r$ , where  $p$  is a prime and  $r$  is positive integer.  
Inserting  $n=p^r$  in (1), the result is ${\textstyle \frac{p^{r+1}-1}{p-1} = 2p^r - 2}$ ,

i.e. $(2) \;\; p^r(p - 2) = 2p - 3$ .

Hence  $3|p$ , implying  $p=3$ , which inserted in (2) give us  $3^r = 3$ , yielding  $r=1$ .  So the only solution of (1) is  $n = p^r = 3^1 = 3 = 2^0(2^1 + 1)$ .**Case 2:**  $n=p^r \cdot q^s$ , where  $p,q$  are primes with  $p<q$  and  $r,s$  are positive integers.  
By inserting  $n=p^rq^s$  in (2), we obtain ${\textstyle \frac{p^{r+1}-1}{p-1} \cdot \frac{q^{s+1}-1}{q-1} = 2p^rq^s - 2}$ ,

i.e. $(p^{r+1} - 1)(q^{s+1} - 1) = 2(p^rq^s - 1)(p - 1)(q - 1)$ ,

which is equivalent to $(3) \;\; p^rq^s(pq - 2p - 2q + 2) = 2(p - 1)(q - 1) - p^{r+1} - q^{s+1} + 1$ . 

The RHS of (3) is $2(p - 1)(q - 1) - p^{r+1} - q^{s+1} + 1$   $= 2pq - p^{r+1} - q^{s+1} - 2(p + q) + 3$  $\leq 2pq - p^2 - q^2 - 2(p + q) + 3$  since  $r,s \geq 1$  $= -(p - q)^2 - 2(p + q) + 3$  $< 0$  

since  $p,q > 1$ .  Therefore  $pq - 2p - 2q + 2 < 0$  by (3), i.e.  $(4) \;\; (p - 2)(q - 2) < 2$ .

If  $p \neq 2$ , then  $p \geq 3$  and  $q \geq 5$ , which implies  $(p - 2)(q - 2) \geq 1 \cdot 3 = 3$ , contradicting (4).  Consequently  $p=2$ , which inserted in (3) result in $-2^{r+1}q^s = 2(q - 1) - 2^{r+1} - q^{s+1} + 1$ ,

i.e.  ${\textstyle 2^{r+1} = \frac{q^{s+1} - 2q + 1}{q^s - 1} = q - \frac{q-1}{q^s-1}}$ .

Therefore  ${\textstyle \frac{q - 1}{q^s - 1} \in \mathbb{N}}$ , implying  $q^s \leq q$ .  Hence  $s=1$  and  $2^{r+1} = q - 1$ , yielding  $n=p^rq^s = 2^rq = 2^r(2^{r+1}-1)$ , where  $2^{r+1}+1=q$  is a prime.

Summa summarum, these two cases give us  $n=2^k(2^{k+1} + 1)$ , where  $k$  is a non-negative integer and  $2^{k+1} + 1$  is a prime, as the only possible solutions of equation (1).  These are indeed solutions of  $(1)$  since  $\sigma(n) = \sigma(2^k(2^{k+1} + 1)) = \sigma(2^k) \cdot \sigma(2^{k+1} + 1) = (2^{k+1} - 1)(2^{k+1} + 2) = 2n - 2$ . **q.e.d.**

stem_md:
Determine the smallest real constant  $c$  such that
\[\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left ( \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}x_j \right )^2\leq c\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_k^2\]
for all positive integers  $n$  and all positive real numbers  $x_1,\cdots ,x_n$ .
solution_md:
A solution hasn't been posted yet, so I will post a solution that utilizes Cauchy Balancing.  

Note that  $ \left(\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j = 1}^{k}x_j\right)^2 \le \left(\sum_{j = 1}^{k}\frac{c_j}{k^2}\right)\left(\sum_{j = 1}^{k}\frac{x_j^2}{c_j}\right) $  for any  $ c_1, c_2, \dots, c_n \in \mathbb{R}^{+}. $   Therefore 
\[ \sum_{k=1}^{n}\left ( \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}x_j \right )^2 \le \sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{j = 1}^{k}\frac{c_j}{k^2}\right)\left(\sum_{j = 1}^{k}\frac{x_j^2}{c_j}\right) = \sum_{k = 1}^{n}a_kx_k^2 \]
Where  $ a_k = \frac{c_1 + c_2 + \dots + c_k}{c_kk^2} + \frac{c_1 + c_2 + \dots + c_{k + 1}}{c_k(k + 1)^2} + \dots + \frac{c_1 + c_2 + \dots + c_n}{c_kn^2} $  for all  $ k \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\}. $   By letting  $ c_k = \sqrt{k} - \sqrt{k - 1} $  we find that  $ a_k = \frac{1}{\sqrt{k} - \sqrt{k - 1}}\sum_{j = k}^{n}j^{-\frac{3}{2}} \le (\sqrt{k} + \sqrt{k - 1})\int_{k - 1}^{n}j^{-\frac{3}{2}} = 2(\sqrt{k} + \sqrt{k - 1})\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{k - 1}} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\right) $  for all  $ k \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\}. $ Letting  $ n $  go to infinity we see that  $ \boxed{c = 4} $  works and is optimal.

stem_md: Let $p$ be an odd prime number. Determine all pairs of polynomials $f$ and $g$ from $\mathbb{Z}[X]$ such that \[f(g(X))=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1} X^k = \Phi_p(X).\]
solution_md:
Let  $\omega$  be a primitive  $n$ -th root of  $1$ . (in our case any root except 1). Suppose there exists  $f,g$  with  $\deg f>1, \deg g>1$ . 
Clearly  $f(g(\omega^k))=0, k=1,2,\ldots,p-1$ . Since  $\deg f<p-1$ , it's not possible all  $g(\omega^k),k=1,2,\ldots,p-1$  to be pairwise different. 
Thus, there exist  $i,j, 1\le i<j\le p-1$  with  $g(\omega^i)=g(\omega^j)$ . 
Hence  $\omega$  is a root of  $P(x)=g(x^i)-g(x^j)$ , where we consider  $P(x)$  overe the field  $\mathbb{Z}_p$ , or one can imagine that all monomials of  $P$  are reduced to have degree less or equal to  $p-1$ . 
Since  $\Phi_p(x)$  is the minimal polynomial having  $\omega$  as a root, there are only two possibilities: 
1)  $P(x)\equiv \Phi_p(x)$ , 
2)  $P(x) \equiv 0$ . 
The first case is impossible since  $P$  doesn't contain a monomial  $x^0$ . Let's consider the second case. 
Denote  $A=\{k\in \mathbb{Z}_p \mid g \text{ contains the monomial }x^k  \}$ . Then,  $g(x^i)\equiv g(x^j)$  implies
\[i\cdot A=k\cdot A\]
Hence, if one denote  $\ell=i\cdot k^{-1}$ , it holds:
\[\ell \cdot A=A,\,\,\,\,\, \ell \neq 1\]
For  $m=\max A$  it must hold  $ \ell \cdot m \leq m$  (over  $\mathbb{Z}_p$ ), hence  $ \ell \cdot m = m$ , which is impossible.
